course.title: Software Testing and Quality
course.description: How to decide what to test, write tests that can fail for the right reasons, and judge a suite and a release by evidence instead of habit.
course.audience: A capable adult who can read and write basic Python, as taught in the existing courses, and has built or maintained small programs.

paragraphs: A passing test shows that some inputs gave the expected results, and little more. This course starts from that limit and asks how to choose the inputs, write the checks and read the evidence so that a green run means as much as it can. The examples are small Python functions, tests with assert, short SQL queries and a handful of numbers, and each lesson says what a technique shows and what it leaves out.

The first lessons cover what a test can claim, how to write a readable deterministic unit test, and how to choose inputs by equivalence classes, boundary values and decision tables. They are followed by coverage and mutation testing, test doubles that remove the clock, the network and the database from a unit test, and properties that generated inputs check on thousands of cases. The middle of the course follows the cycle of red, green and refactor, and the pyramid of unit, integration and end-to-end tests with its arithmetic of speed and flakiness.

The last three lessons widen the view. They test data with queries and services with contracts, read response times as percentiles and size capacity with Little's law, and turn to bug reports, severity and priority, defect detection percentage and the place of testing in a delivery pipeline. Each lesson ends with a short skill check, and the numbers in them are calculations you can repeat.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what a passing test does and does not show.
You'll be able to write a small deterministic unit test and run it.
You'll be able to choose inputs by partitions and boundaries.
You'll be able to compute coverage, mutation score, flake probability and defect detection percentage.
You'll be able to place tests at the right level and read percentiles and Little's law for performance.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Python for Data Analysis and How Computers Solve Problems: you should be able to read short Python functions, and a little SQL helps in one lesson.

modules.title: What testing can tell you
modules.description: What a test claims, how to write one, and how to choose inputs that matter.

modules.title: Techniques
modules.description: Measuring what tests exercise, isolating what they test, and finding what example-based tests miss.

modules.title: Strategy and non-functional quality
modules.description: Balancing test levels, testing data, speed and load, and measuring quality and process.

concepts.title: Test oracle
concepts.summary: The source of the expected result against which actual behaviour is compared.

concepts.title: Verification versus validation
concepts.summary: Verification asks whether we built it right against the specification; validation asks whether we built the right thing.

concepts.title: Limits of testing
concepts.summary: Testing can reveal defects but cannot prove their absence, because inputs are too many to try.

concepts.title: Arrange, act, assert
concepts.summary: Set up the inputs, call the unit, check one behaviour.

concepts.title: Deterministic test
concepts.summary: Given the same code it always gives the same result, independent of time, order or network.

concepts.title: Behaviour naming
concepts.summary: A test name states the situation and the expected result, so a failure explains itself.

concepts.title: Equivalence partitioning
concepts.summary: Group inputs that the program should treat the same and test one from each group.

concepts.title: Boundary value analysis
concepts.summary: Test at and next to the edges of each partition, where off-by-one errors live.

concepts.title: Decision table
concepts.summary: A grid of condition combinations and the expected action for each.

concepts.title: Line and branch coverage
concepts.summary: Line coverage counts statements run; branch coverage counts decision outcomes taken.

concepts.title: Mutation testing
concepts.summary: Small deliberate faults (mutants) are planted; tests that fail on them kill them.

concepts.title: Coverage as a target
concepts.summary: A number used as a target stops measuring quality, because tests can run code without checking anything.

concepts.title: Test double
concepts.summary: A stand-in for a real dependency; kinds include stub, fake, mock and spy.

concepts.title: Dependency injection
concepts.summary: The unit receives its dependencies as arguments, so a test can supply doubles.

concepts.title: Over-mocking
concepts.summary: Tests that restate the implementation break on refactoring and prove little.

concepts.title: Property
concepts.summary: A statement that holds for every valid input, such as reversing a list twice returns it.

concepts.title: Shrinking
concepts.summary: A generator reduces a failing input to a minimal one that still fails.

concepts.title: Exploratory testing
concepts.summary: Simultaneous learning, test design and execution guided by the tester's judgement.

concepts.title: Red, green, refactor
concepts.summary: Write a failing test, make it pass in the simplest way, then improve the design with tests green.

concepts.title: Refactoring
concepts.summary: Changing structure without changing behaviour, which tests must confirm.

concepts.title: Regression test
concepts.summary: A test written for a fixed bug so it cannot return.

concepts.title: Test levels
concepts.summary: Unit tests check one piece, integration tests check pieces together, end-to-end tests check a user journey.

concepts.title: Test pyramid
concepts.summary: Many fast low-level tests and few slow high-level ones keep feedback fast and failures local.

concepts.title: Flaky test
concepts.summary: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code.

concepts.title: Data quality check
concepts.summary: A query that asserts a rule about data, such as uniqueness, non-null or valid range.

concepts.title: Contract test
concepts.summary: A test that a provider and a consumer agree on the shape and meaning of messages.

concepts.title: Test data
concepts.summary: Small, deliberate, independent data created per test, never shared mutable data.

concepts.title: Percentile
concepts.summary: The p-th percentile is the value at or below which p per cent of observations fall; the mean can hide the slow tail.

concepts.title: Little's law
concepts.summary: Average concurrency L equals arrival rate lambda times average time in system W.

concepts.title: Non-functional tests
concepts.summary: Tests of performance, security, accessibility, reliability and usability, which have thresholds rather than exact answers.

concepts.title: Severity versus priority
concepts.summary: Severity is the impact of a defect; priority is the order in which it should be fixed.

concepts.title: Defect detection percentage
concepts.summary: Defects found before release as a share of all defects found before and after.

concepts.title: Shift left and right
concepts.summary: Test early (reviews, unit tests) and also observe production (monitoring, canaries), since neither alone finds everything.

lessons.title: What a test can and cannot show

steps.headline: A passing test shows that one input gave the expected result, and nothing about the inputs that were not tried.

lead.text: Each row in the figure is one **test**: an input is given to the function, the result is noted, and the result is compared with the result that was expected. The function is_leap returns True when year % 4 == 0, and the five tests give True for 2024, 2020 and 2000 and False for 2023 and 2021. All five rows pass, and yet the function is wrong.

The sixth view shows why. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year *except* when it is a century, and a century counts only when it is also divisible by 400. The year 1900 is a century that 400 does not divide, so it was not a leap year, but 1900 % 4 is 0 and the function answers True. None of the five inputs was a century of that kind, so none of them could have noticed.

afterFigure.text: Five passes were therefore *true* reports, and each said exactly what it had checked: that the function behaves as expected at that one input. The mistake lies in reading five passes as a statement about all years. What a suite can honestly claim is limited by the inputs it chose, a limit that the rest of this course keeps returning to.

lead.text: Add one more test to the five in the figure: is_leap(1900) is expected to be False. Before running anything, work out what the function returns for 1900, and decide how many of the six tests will pass.

reveal.text: The function returns True for 1900, because 1900 % 4 is 0, so the sixth test fails and five of six pass. The suite is still wrong; it now reports it.

steps.headline: Every test needs an expected result from somewhere other than the code under test, and that source is called the oracle.

lead.text: A test has three parts, and the figure labels them. The *input* is what the function is given, the *action* is the call to the function, and the *expected result* is what the function should return. The comparison between the actual result and the expected result is what produces a pass or a fail.

The expected result has to come from somewhere, and in the figure it comes from the calendar rule that centuries are leap years only when divisible by 400. That source is called the test's **oracle**. It might be a written rule, a table of known answers, a hand calculation, or another program that is trusted more than the one under test, such as Python's calendar.isleap. What matters is that the oracle is *independent* of the code being checked: if the expected value is copied from what the function currently returns, the test can never disagree with it.

afterFigure.text: Choosing the oracle is therefore the hard part of writing a test. Choosing an input is easy, but knowing what the correct output for that input is requires knowledge that the code does not have. When no oracle is available, as with a program that predicts weather, the tests have to be weaker, and a later lesson on properties looks at what can be checked instead.

lead.text: A new sorting function is tested by running it on a list and also running Python's built-in sorted on the same list. Name the role that the built-in plays.

reveal.text: Because sorted is trusted more than the new function, a disagreement points at the new function. If both were wrong in the same way, the test would still pass.

steps.headline: Trying every input is out of reach even for a small function, so a suite always samples.

lead.text: An obvious reply to the leap-year fault is to test *every* year. For is_leap that is possible, since there are only a few thousand years that matter. But a function that takes two 32-bit integers, such as one that adds two numbers or compares two ids, accepts 2^32 values for each argument, and every value of the first can be paired with every value of the second. The number of pairs is 2^32 × 2^32, which is 2^64.

That number is 18,446,744,073,709,551,616. The figure shows how fast it grows: two 8-bit integers give 2^16, or 65,536 pairs, which a computer finishes in a fraction of a millisecond, and two 16-bit integers give 2^32, about 4.3 billion pairs, which take about 4.3 seconds at a billion tests a second. Each doubling of the width *squares* the count, and the pair of 32-bit integers takes about 585 years.

afterFigure.text: Checking all inputs is called **exhaustive testing**, and for almost any real program it cannot be done. Edsger Dijkstra put the consequence in 1970, in his Notes on Structured Programming: testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence. A test suite is therefore a sample of the input space, and the useful question is how well the sample was chosen.

steps.headline: Work out how long exhaustive testing of two 32-bit integers takes at a billion tests a second.

workedSteps.text: Count the input pairs: each argument takes 2^32 values, and the pairs multiply.
Divide the number of tests by the rate to get the time in seconds.
A year of 365.25 days contains 365.25 × 24 × 3600 seconds.
Divide the seconds by the seconds in a year.

lead.text: A function takes two 12-bit integers. Use the same reasoning as before to decide whether exhaustive testing is feasible, starting from how many pairs there are.

reveal.text: Sixteen million pairs is small enough for exhaustive testing, at about a hundredth of a second at a billion tests a second. Whether exhaustive testing is feasible depends on the width of the inputs.

steps.headline: Verification asks whether the product matches its specification, and validation asks whether the specification matches the need.

lead.text: Passing every test against a specification still leaves a second question open. A **specification** is a written statement of what a product should do, and checking the product against it is called **verification**: was it built right? The tests for is_leap verify the function against the calendar rule.

Suppose a tax form follows its specification to the letter, but the specification asks for gross income where people need the form to work out what they owe after allowances. Every check against the specification passes, and the form is still of no use. Checking that the product satisfies the need of those who will use it is called **validation**: was the right thing built? The figure puts the three things side by side, with verification as the arrow from specification to product and validation as the arrow from need to product.

afterFigure.text: The two checks fail in different ways and are repaired in different places. A verification failure sends the team back to the code, whereas a validation failure sends it back to the specification and to the people the product is for. No amount of unit testing answers the second, because every unit test takes the specification as its oracle.

diagram.alt: Three boxes in a row: the user's need, the specification and the product. Verification is an arrow from the specification to the product. Validation is an arrow from the need to the product.

lead.text: Read the scenario carefully, and decide whether the product is being compared with its specification or with what users need.

reveal.text: The product matched the specification, so verification passes. Only watching real users, or asking them, would have shown that fractions were missing.

steps.headline: A suite is worth having for more than finding bugs, which is why its value does not fall to zero when it finds none.

lead.text: If tests cannot prove correctness, it is fair to ask what they are for. Software Engineering at Google gives several answers, and they apply well beyond that company. A suite gives *confidence* that the behaviours it describes still hold. It guards against **regression**, which is the return of behaviour that used to work after a change. It *documents* what the code is meant to do in a form that is checked every time it runs. And writing the test first makes the author see the awkwardness of an interface before many others depend on it.

Testing is also wider than running code. Reading a requirement and finding that two rules contradict each other is a test of the idea, done before a line is written, and the standard glossaries count reviews and other checks that never run the program as *static* testing. The cheapest defect to repair is the one found while it is still a sentence in a document.

afterFigure.text: So a passing suite is evidence, and the strength of the evidence depends on the inputs chosen, on the independence of the oracle, and on whether the specification was the right one. The next lesson turns to the first of these in practice and writes a small test.

lead.text: A team reads the requirements for a booking system before any code is written, and finds two rules that contradict each other. Decide whether this counts as testing.

reveal.text: A review is static testing: it finds the defect in a document without executing anything, which is usually the cheapest time to find one.

lessons.orientation: What a passing test establishes, where its expected result comes from, and why the number of inputs limits testing.
lessons.reviewLabel: What a test can and cannot show
lessons.nextAction: Write a small, readable, deterministic unit test for is_leap with arrange, act and assert.

blocks.text: A function named is_leap returns True when year % 4 == 0, and five tests check it: 2024, 2020 and 2000 are expected to give True, and 2023 and 2021 to give False. All five pass, and a suite that reports five passes out of five looks like good evidence that the function is right.

The function is wrong. A year divisible by 4 is not a leap year when it is a century that 400 does not divide, and 1900 is such a year, but none of the five inputs was a century of that kind. What a passing test tells you depends entirely on which inputs were tried and where the expected results came from.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a passing test does and does not show, name the oracle in a test, and tell verification from validation.
intro.whyItMatters: Knowing what a suite can claim tells you how far to trust a green run.

recap.keyIdea: A passing test shows that one input gave the expected result, and a suite is a sample of inputs checked against an oracle, not a proof of correctness.

blocks.text: A test pairs an input with an expected result drawn from an independent **oracle**, and the 2^64 input pairs of even a two-argument function mean that a suite can only sample. Verification checks the product against its specification and validation checks it against the need, so a suite can pass both the five tests and the specification and still describe the wrong thing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson writes a first unit test for is_leap, names it by behaviour and makes it fail on purpose.

lessons.title: Writing a good unit test

steps.headline: A unit test arranges its input, acts by calling the unit once, and asserts one expected behaviour.

lead.text: The test in the figure has three lines, and each does one job. The first, year = 1900, **arranges** the test by setting up what the code needs, here a single input. The second, result = is_leap(year), **acts**: it calls the code under test, and only once. The third, assert result is False, **asserts**, which means that it states what must be true of the result. This division is called *arrange, act, assert*, and tests that follow it can be read in seconds because the reader always knows which line is which.

The assert statement is Python's own check. If the condition after assert is true, nothing happens and the program carries on. If it is false, Python raises an **AssertionError**, which stops the test and is reported as a failure. The word *unit* in unit test refers to the size of the thing under test, a function or a small class, in contrast with a whole program.

afterFigure.text: Keep the act line to a single call. When a test calls the code twice and checks something at the end, a failure leaves you guessing which call caused it. Keeping arrange, act and assert separate also leaves a place for a second input, since the arrange section can be changed without touching the other two.

diagram.alt: A test function named test_century_not_divisible_by_400_is_not_leap with three lines in its body: year = 1900, result = is_leap(year) and assert result is False. In the second view the lines are labelled arrange, act and assert.

lead.text: Before the next screen explains how failures are reported, read this snippet and decide what the print call will show.

reveal.text: A false assert raises AssertionError, and the text after the comma travels inside it. The next screen shows how that text appears when nothing catches the exception.

steps.headline: A failing assert stops with a message, and a good message names the expected result.

lead.text: Run the check in the first view and nothing appears at all, which is how a passing assert behaves. In the second view the function returns True for 1900, so the condition is false and Python reports an **AssertionError**. The report ends with the message that was written after the comma in the assert, and the lines above it show the file and line number of the check that failed.

The message is worth writing because it is what you read first. A bare failure says that something was false, whereas a message such as “1900 is not a leap year” says what was expected, so that you can tell whether the code or the test is at fault. Test frameworks such as Python's unittest print the values of both sides when you use their comparison methods, which is a second reason to prefer them as suites grow, and the next screens keep to plain assert.

afterFigure.text: Reading a failure means asking three things in order: which check failed, what was expected, and what was actually returned. Only then is it worth opening the code. A failure whose message answers the first two saves most of the effort.

lead.text: Work out what the broken function year % 4 == 0 returns for each of the four years, and compare each with what the test expects.

reveal.text: The two failing tests are the two centuries that 400 does not divide. Tests at 2000 and 2023 pass against the broken function, so they cannot tell it apart from the correct one.

steps.headline: A test name should state the situation and the expected result, so that a failure explains itself.

lead.text: The same failure can be reported under two names, and the figure puts them side by side. Under the name test1 the report says that something failed and leaves you to open the file. Under test_century_not_divisible_by_400_is_not_leap it says that a century not divisible by 400 was expected not to be a leap year, which is the *situation* and the *expected result* together. A name that carries both is a **behaviour name**.

Behaviour names have a second use, which is that a list of them reads as a specification of the code. A reader who scans the names of the tests for an order form, such as rejects_negative_quantity, accepts_zero_discount and totals_include_postage, learns what the form does without reading any body. The names tend to be long, and that is acceptable, since nobody types a test name twice.

afterFigure.text: Names also expose tests that try to do too much. If a name needs the word and, such as accepts_valid_dates_and_rejects_empty, the test is checking two behaviours and is better split in two, which is the subject of the next screens.

lead.text: Choose the name that gives a reader the situation and the expected result.

reveal.text: The chosen name states both, and the others leave out the situation, the expected result or both.

lead.text: Before reading about why tests should check one behaviour, work out how many of the three assert lines in a test run when the second one fails.

reveal.text: The exception ends the test at the second line. The third check never runs, so a test with many asserts reports only its first failure.

steps.headline: A test with one reason to fail points to one cause, and a test of internals breaks when behaviour has not changed.

lead.text: Because a failed assert ends the test, a test with several asserts reports only the first problem and hides the rest. A test with a single behaviour has a single reason to fail, so a failure points to one cause. Splitting a test of three behaviours into three tests costs a few lines and means that all three results appear in one run.

A related risk comes from what the test looks at. A test that asserts the *behaviour*, such as the value returned for 1900, keeps passing when the code inside is rewritten, provided the answer stays the same. A test that reaches into the internals, checking which helper was called or what a private variable holds, fails when the code is tidied even though nothing visible has changed. Software Engineering at Google makes the same point, advising tests of the public interface through the calls a user would make.

afterFigure.text: Failures of this second kind teach people to distrust the suite, because a red result no longer signals a defect. The aim is for every red to mean that behaviour changed.

steps.headline: A test that has never been seen to fail may be unable to fail, so run it once against broken code.

lead.text: A passing test is only good evidence if the test would have failed on wrong code. Some tests cannot: an assert whose condition is always true, a test whose body never runs because of a typing slip in its name, or a comparison of a value with itself. All of them are green and all of them check nothing.

The remedy is to see the test fail on purpose, in the order shown in the figure. Write the test, run it against code that is deliberately wrong, such as the version that tests only year % 4 == 0, and watch it fail with the message you expect. This is called the **red step**, since test runners show a failure in red. Then run it against the correct code and watch it pass. A test that has been seen to go red for the right reason has shown that it can tell good code from bad.

afterFigure.text: The check takes under a minute and is most worth doing for a test that was written *after* the code, when the code already passes and nothing has ever made the test fail.

diagram.alt: A test box and a code box with an arrow between them. With the code as written the result is green and the test passes. With the code broken on purpose, by using year % 4 == 0 alone, the result is red and the test fails.

steps.headline: Add a test for 2100 and show that it can fail.

workedSteps.text: Write the test with a behaviour name, one input and one assert.
workedSteps.math: def test_2100_is_not_leap(): assert is_leap(2100) is False

workedSteps.text: Run it against the deliberately broken function year % 4 == 0. The function returns True for 2100, so the assert fails.
Replace the body with the corrected rule, year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0), and run the test again.
workedSteps.math: 2100 % 100 != 0 is False and 2100 % 400 != 0, so the result is False

workedSteps.text: The result is False, which equals the expected value, so the test passes: red against the broken code, green against the correct code.

steps.headline: A deterministic test depends only on its code and its arguments, never on the clock, the order of tests or the network.

lead.text: A test is **deterministic** when, for the same code, it always gives the same result. The test in the figure reads the current year inside age_in_years, so it passes through 2026 and fails on 1 January 2027 although no line of code has changed. The same happens when a test uses random numbers without a fixed seed, depends on running after another test, or calls a network service that is sometimes slow.

The cure is to turn each hidden input into an *argument*, as the second view does: age_in_years(born, today) takes the date as a parameter, and the test supplies date(2026, 6, 1). Nothing the test depends on can change under it. A random generator can be given a fixed seed so that it produces the same numbers every run. The lesson on test doubles returns to how to do this for clocks and services that cannot be passed in so easily.

afterFigure.text: Non-deterministic tests are damaging because the failures cannot be reproduced, and a failure that cannot be reproduced is soon ignored.

lead.text: The age test from the figure is run on 1 January 2027 against the version that reads the clock. Apply what you saw on the timeline to a new value.

reveal.text: The test's expected value, 36, was right for 2026 only. Supplying the date as an argument would have kept the answer at 36 for the date given.

lessons.orientation: Write a test with arrange, act and assert, name it by behaviour and make it deterministic.
lessons.nextAction: Choose test inputs by equivalence partitions and boundaries instead of by guesswork.

blocks.text: The corrected function returns year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0), and 1900 should now give False. The way to find out is to write that claim down as a test that a program can run, and Python's assert statement does this: if the condition after it is true nothing happens, and if it is false the program stops with an AssertionError.

A test written with assert is an ordinary function, and the one in the figure has the shape that nearly every good unit test has. It sets up an input, calls the code under test once, and states what must be true of the result, and its name says which situation it covers, so that a failure explains itself before the file is opened.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a small unit test with assert, name it by behaviour, run it and read the failure, and remove hidden inputs such as the clock.
intro.whyItMatters: A readable test that is seen to fail first is far more useful than one that merely passes.

recap.keyIdea: A good unit test arranges its input, acts once, asserts one behaviour under a name that states it, and has been seen to fail, with no hidden dependence on time or order.

blocks.text: You wrote tests with assert, read an AssertionError from the bottom up, and saw that a failed assert ends the test, so one behaviour per test keeps every failure visible. A test is trustworthy once it has been seen to go red for the right reason and cannot be changed by the date or by the order in which tests run.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks which inputs to give such tests, so that a handful of them can stand for the thousands that cannot be run.

lessons.title: Choosing inputs: partitions and boundaries

lead.text: A pricing function should give the standard rate to ages 18 to 65 inclusive, and by mistake it uses age > 18 and age < 65. It is tested at 10, 40 and 80. Work out how many of the three tests fail.

reveal.text: None fail, which is why testing at ages like these gives false comfort. The next screen starts from this observation.

steps.headline: Inputs that the program should treat alike form an equivalence class, and one test from each class is enough to represent it.

lead.text: The rule in the figure divides ages into three groups. Every age under 18 gets the same treatment, every age from 18 to 65 gets another, and every age over 65 gets a third. A group of inputs that the specification says should behave alike is called an **equivalence class**. If the program really does treat the members alike, one test in the class tells you about all of them, since a second member would take the same path through the code.

Choosing a single representative from each class is called **equivalence partitioning**. It replaces the question “which ages should I try?”, which has a hundred answers, with “what are the classes?”, which has three. The figure's second view marks one age in each class, 10, 40 and 80, and those three tests do cover every kind of behaviour the rule describes.

afterFigure.text: The word *represent* is carrying an assumption, which is that members of a class behave alike, and the assumption comes from the specification, not from the code. A mistake in the code can still make one member of a class behave differently, and the previous screen's mistaken comparison does exactly that to two values, 18 and 65, which the next screens deal with.

diagram.alt: A number line of ages from 0 to 100 divided into three classes: under 18, 18 to 65 which pay the standard rate, and over 65. A second view marks one test age in each class, 10, 40 and 80. A third view marks 17, 18, 65 and 66, which sit at the edges.

lead.text: Apply the idea to a different rule: a form field accepts whole numbers from 1 to 99. Decide what the classes are before you count.

reveal.text: The count of values in a class does not matter; what matters is the number of classes. The values at the edges of classes are looked at next.

steps.headline: Off-by-one mistakes live at the edges of a class, so the values at and next to each edge are the best tests.

lead.text: The figure's second view shows the mistake from the first screen. Replacing >= with > moves the start of the standard rate from 18 to 19, so exactly one value, 18, is handled wrongly. Tests in the middle of a class cannot see this, because the correct and mistaken code agree on 10, 40 and 80. A value exactly at an edge is called a **boundary value**, and it is here that a mistake in a comparison changes the result.

**Boundary value analysis** tests the values at and next to each edge. For ages 18 to 65 inclusive, the edges are 18 and 65, and the *two-value* method takes the edge and the value just outside it: 17 and 18 at one end, 65 and 66 at the other, which gives four tests. The *three-value* method adds the value just inside each edge, 19 and 64, and gives six.

afterFigure.text: Glenford Myers popularised both techniques in The Art of Software Testing in 1979. Their appeal is the cost: four tests find every one-off error in the two comparisons, where a hundred random ages would very probably find none.

diagram.alt: Four boxes for ages 16, 17, 18 and 19. With the correct test age >= 18 the ages 18 and 19 are charged the standard rate. With the mistaken test age > 18 the age 18 is charged the child rate, shown in red.

lead.text: Name the kind of value that the mistaken comparison gets wrong.

reveal.text: The name applies to any value where behaviour changes, and a program can have many of them.

steps.headline: List the boundary tests for ages 18 to 65 inclusive, with the three-value method.

workedSteps.text: Find the edges of the valid class. The standard rate begins at 18 and ends at 65.
Take the value just outside each edge, which is where a wrong comparison puts a value on the wrong side.
Take the value just inside each edge for the three-value method.
Combine the edge values with their neighbours and count them, checking that no value appears twice.

steps.headline: Invalid input forms classes of its own, and boundaries are every place behaviour changes, not just the edges of the valid range.

lead.text: A rule says what to do with good input, and it usually says nothing about the rest, yet the rest arrives. For an age field, a negative number, text such as "abc" and an empty value are all inputs that the program must do *something* with, and each is a separate class because the program should respond to each differently, for instance with an error message. Many defects live here: a crash on an empty field is common and survives any number of tests of valid ages.

The edges of the valid range are not the only boundaries either. Zero is a boundary because the sign of the number changes there. The largest number the field can hold is a boundary because arithmetic can overflow. Anywhere the behaviour changes is a place to test on both sides of the change, and the list of classes in the figure is the starting point for that search.

afterFigure.text: So the test set for the age rule has valid classes with their boundary values and invalid classes with at least one value each. Together they make a set that can be listed in full and run in a second.

diagram.alt: Boxes for the age classes. The first view shows three valid classes: under 18, 18 to 65 and over 65. The second adds three invalid classes: a negative number, text that is not a number, and empty input.

lead.text: Count the valid classes and the invalid classes in the figure, and give the total.

reveal.text: Each of the six classes needs a test with its own expected result, and the three invalid ones are checked for an error rather than a rate.

steps.headline: When several conditions combine, a decision table lists every combination and the action each should give.

lead.text: Partitions and boundaries deal with one input at a time. Rules often combine several conditions, such as a loan that is approved only when the applicant is employed *and* has an income of at least 20,000. A **decision table** has one column for each combination of the conditions, with the action each combination should produce, and the figure shows one for two conditions. Employed with high income is approved, employed with low income is referred to a person, and anyone not employed is rejected whatever the income.

The table makes the rule complete, since a missing column shows a combination that the specification forgot, and it makes the tests easy to choose, because each column is one test. It also shows the cost of combining conditions: each one doubles the number of columns, so three conditions give eight combinations and the third view of the figure fits them in. Boundary values apply to each condition as well, so the income condition would also be tested just below and at 20,000.

afterFigure.text: Beyond about four conditions the table becomes too large to read, and the usual response is to split the rule into smaller tables rather than to leave out columns.

diagram.alt: A decision table for a loan rule. With two conditions, employed and income of at least 20,000, there are four columns of yes and no. Approve needs both yes, refer when employed with low income, reject otherwise. With a third condition, no existing debt, there are eight columns.

lead.text: Use the doubling idea from the figure to decide how large the table gets when a third condition is added.

reveal.text: The count grows as a power of two, which is the same arithmetic as the input counts in the first lesson.

lead.text: A bulk discount applies to orders of 100 items or more, a rule with a single edge instead of a range. Apply the two-value method to it.

reveal.text: Counting edges first is the reliable way to count boundary tests: each edge gives two.

lessons.orientation: Divide inputs into classes, add boundary values, and tabulate combinations of conditions.
lessons.nextAction: Measure how much of the code a test set runs, and ask whether that number can be trusted.

blocks.text: A pricing rule gives the standard rate to ages 18 to 65 inclusive. If the code says age > 18 and age < 65 by mistake, tests at ages 10, 40 and 80 all pass, and so would a hundred other ages chosen from the middle of the three groups, because the mistake changes only two values.

Choosing inputs is therefore a matter of knowing where mistakes cluster and not of choosing a large number of them. The figure divides the ages into the groups that the rule treats alike, and the values at the edges between groups are the ones that detect the mistake.

diagram.alt: A number line of ages from 0 to 100 divided into three classes: under 18, 18 to 65 which pay the standard rate, and over 65. A second view marks one test age in each class, 10, 40 and 80. A third view marks 17, 18, 65 and 66, which sit at the edges.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose test inputs by equivalence classes and boundary values, and list combinations of conditions in a decision table.
intro.whyItMatters: A short test set chosen by class and boundary finds more faults than a long random one.

recap.keyIdea: Test one value from each equivalence class and the values at and next to each boundary, and use a decision table where conditions combine.

blocks.text: Equivalence partitioning replaces many inputs with one representative per class, and boundary value analysis adds the values at the edges, where comparisons go wrong. Invalid input forms classes of its own, and a decision table lists the 2^n combinations that n conditions give.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks how much of the code a test set runs, and why a high figure can still hide a poor suite.

lessons.title: Coverage and mutation testing

lead.text: The function f in the next figure has six lines: r = 0, if a, r += 1, if b, r += 2 and return r. Before looking at any measure, follow a single call, f(True, False), and count the lines that run.

reveal.text: The line under if b is skipped, so five of six lines run. The next screen turns counts like this into measures.

steps.headline: Line coverage counts the lines that ran, and branch coverage counts the outcomes of each decision that were taken.

lead.text: A tool that measures **coverage** watches the code while a suite runs and reports which parts ran. **Line coverage** is the share of lines that ran: for f(True, False) it is 5 of 6, or 83%, since the line r += 2 never ran. **Branch coverage** counts something finer. Each if has two outcomes, true and false, so the two ifs in f give four, and a branch is covered only when its outcome has actually been taken.

The figure's first view shows why the two differ. The call f(True, True) runs every line, so line coverage is 100%, but both ifs were true and neither false outcome has been taken, which makes branch coverage 2 of 4, or 50%. A second call, f(False, False), takes the other two outcomes, and the third view shows the pair reaching all four. Branch coverage is the stricter measure for this reason, since reaching every line does not mean that every decision was tested both ways.

afterFigure.text: Both measures answer the same kind of question, *which parts of the code did the tests run?* A part that never ran cannot have been checked by any test, and low coverage therefore reliably identifies code that is untested.

lead.text: Work out which of the four outcomes each of the two calls takes, and then count the distinct ones.

reveal.text: Two calls are enough here, but only because they were chosen to differ at every decision.

steps.headline: Coverage shows what ran and not what was checked, so a test with no assertion can reach any figure.

lead.text: Imagine that the second branch of f has a fault and adds 3 where it should add 2. The figure's first view runs f(True, True) in a test that makes no assertion. Every line runs, the test passes, and a report would show 100% line coverage. The fault is not noticed, because nothing compared the returned value, 4, with the expected one, 3.

The second view adds a single assertion, and the same call now fails and reveals the fault. The coverage figure has not changed at all, which is the point: coverage measures the *execution* of code, and an assertion is what turns execution into a check. A suite can therefore reach complete coverage by calling every function and checking nothing.

afterFigure.text: This is a limit on what the figure means, not a reason to drop the measure. A high figure is compatible with a weak suite, but a low figure is still a reliable sign of code that no test has run.

lead.text: Read the claim carefully, since the question concerns what the figure measures.

reveal.text: The figure describes execution only. Whether the results were checked is a separate matter, which the next screen turns to.

steps.headline: Mutation testing plants small faults in the code and counts how many of them the tests notice.

lead.text: To find out whether a suite would notice a fault, you can plant faults and see. A tool makes many copies of the code, each with one small change, such as replacing r += 2 with r += 3 or if a with if not a. Each changed copy is called a **mutant**. The suite is run against every mutant, and a mutant that makes some test fail is said to be **killed**, whereas a mutant that every test passes has **survived**.

The **mutation score** is the percentage of mutants killed. In the figure one test, assert f(True, True) == 3, kills six of eight mutants, a score of 75%. The two survivors replace a condition with True, which makes no difference when both conditions were true in the first place. A survivor is a specific gap: the second view adds a test of f(False, False), which kills both, and the score reaches 100%.

afterFigure.text: Mutation testing is slower than coverage, because the suite runs once for each mutant, but it measures the thing that coverage leaves out. A survivor can also be an *equivalent* mutant, one whose behaviour is the same as the original's, so a score below 100% is not always a gap.

lead.text: Name a copy of the code with one deliberate small change made to it.

reveal.text: Mutants are made by a tool, not a person, so that a suite can be measured without bias about where its weak points are.

steps.headline: Score the suite that has the single test assert f(True, True) == 3.

workedSteps.text: Run the test on the original code. f(True, True) = 3, so the test passes, as it must for the comparison to mean anything.
Run it on each of the eight mutants and note which make it fail. Mutant 5, if a replaced by if True, returns 3 when a is already True, so the test cannot tell it apart.
Mutant 6 is the same kind of change to if b. Every other mutant gives a value other than 3.
Count the killed mutants and divide by the total, as a percentage.

steps.headline: A number used as a target stops measuring quality, because the quickest way to raise it is to run code without checking it.

lead.text: Suppose a team is told that every change must keep coverage above 90%. The quickest way to meet the target is to add tests that call functions and assert nothing, since coverage falls only when code goes unrun. The number goes up and the suite improves little, as the earlier screen on assertions showed. This effect of a measure losing its meaning once it becomes a target is known as **Goodhart's law**, after the economist Charles Goodhart.

Mutation score resists this better, because a test that checks nothing kills no mutants. It is also easier to understand through its survivors, each of which points at a missing test. The sensible use of both numbers is as *questions* asked of a suite: low coverage says that code is untested, and a survivor says what an assertion should have caught. Software Engineering at Google treats coverage in this way, as a signal to be read alongside the tests and not a gate to be passed.

afterFigure.text: Metrics are most useful when nobody is rewarded for moving them. A team that reads a survivor and writes the missing assertion is using the measure as intended.

lead.text: Apply branch coverage to a different function, with a chain of two decisions. Write down which outcome each call takes before counting.

reveal.text: The one outcome left is reached only by the value 0, a boundary of the kind the previous lesson describes. Coverage and boundary analysis tend to point at the same gaps.

lessons.orientation: Count lines and branch outcomes covered, read a mutation score, and see why coverage can mislead.
lessons.nextAction: Isolate the code under test from slow or unpredictable dependencies with test doubles.

blocks.text: A coverage report counts how much of a program the tests ran. The function f in the figure has six lines and two decisions, and a single call, f(True, True), runs all six lines and takes only half of the four decision outcomes, so the same suite is at once 100% on one measure and 50% on another.

Neither number says whether the results were checked. A test that calls f and asserts nothing would earn the same figures, and the lesson separates what a coverage figure shows from what it leaves out.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute line and branch coverage, read a mutation score, and say why 100% coverage does not mean a well-tested program.
intro.whyItMatters: These figures appear on dashboards and in review, and knowing what they omit stops them being misread.

recap.keyIdea: Coverage shows which code ran, and a mutation score shows how many planted faults the assertions caught, so only the second says anything about the checks.

blocks.text: Line coverage counts statements that ran, branch coverage counts decision outcomes that were taken, and both can reach 100% with no assertion at all. Mutation testing plants small faults and reports the share the tests kill, which exposes weak assertions, and any measure that is turned into a target is soon met without being improved.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson takes up the problem of code that calls the clock, a network or a database, and how a test replaces them.

lessons.title: Isolation and test doubles

lead.text: A function greeting() reads the real clock and answers 'Good morning' before 12:00. A test asserts that it does, and a build server runs the test at every whole hour from 08:00 to 17:00 inclusive. Decide how many of the runs pass.

reveal.text: The test fails in the afternoon although the code never changes. The next screen shows how to take the clock out of the function.

steps.headline: A unit that receives its dependencies as arguments can be tested with any values the test chooses.

lead.text: The function in the first view depends on something outside its arguments, the real clock, and the test cannot set the clock. A thing that a unit relies on but does not itself contain is called a **dependency**: the clock, a network service, a database, the file system and a random number generator are the usual ones. Each makes a test slower, less predictable or both.

The second view changes greeting so that it takes the time as an argument. The test now supplies 09:00 and always gets 'Good morning', whatever the real time is. Handing a unit its dependencies from outside, instead of letting it find them itself, is called **dependency injection**. It can be as plain as an extra parameter, as here, or a constructor argument for a class, and it needs no special library.

afterFigure.text: The previous lesson did the same for age_in_years, which took the date as an argument. Injection is the general form of that move, and it applies to anything that is slow, random or outside the program's control.

lead.text: Name the practice that the second view of the figure demonstrates.

reveal.text: Once a dependency is an argument, the test can give it a stand-in, which is what the next screen classifies.

steps.headline: A test double stands in for a dependency, and its kind depends on what it does with the calls it receives.

lead.text: Whatever the test passes in place of the real dependency is called a **test double**, by analogy with a stunt double in a film. Doubles differ in how much they do, and the four common kinds are named in the figure. A **stub** returns canned answers, so the test decides what the dependency says. A **fake** is a simple but working version of the dependency, such as a dictionary that stores users in memory. A **mock** checks the calls it receives and fails the test if they were not the expected ones. A **spy** records its calls and lets the test inspect them afterwards.

The kinds are easily confused, because tools often call everything a mock. The distinction worth keeping is what the double *does*. A stub or a fake supplies answers and a test then checks the *result* of the unit. A mock or a spy supplies a record of *interactions*, and a test checks that the right calls were made.

afterFigure.text: Software Engineering at Google gives an order of preference that follows from this. Use the real dependency if it is fast and deterministic, then a fake, and keep stubs and interaction checks for the cases where nothing simpler will do.

diagram.alt: A unit under test connected to a test double. Four views name the double: a stub returns a canned answer, a fake is a simple working version, a mock checks the calls made to it, and a spy records the calls it receives.
diagram.caption: Four kinds of test double. Use the buttons to see what each does.

lead.text: Decide what the dependency does in the description, and match it to a kind.

reveal.text: The dependency only supplies an answer, and the test checks the unit's output rather than the calls.

steps.headline: A fake that behaves like the real store lets many tests share one fast, correct stand-in.

lead.text: A user repository normally reads and writes a database, which is slow to set up and shared between tests. A fake replaces it with a Python dictionary: add(user) stores the user under its id and get(id) reads it back, all in memory. The first view of the figure shows the real arrangement, with the database server behind the repository, and the second shows the fake that takes its place.

A fake is more work to write than a stub, since it has to behave like the real thing wherever the tests rely on it, and adding a user with an id that exists must replace it, as in a table keyed by id. The effort is repaid, because one fake serves every test of every unit that uses the repository, and each test builds a fresh one so that no test sees another's data.

afterFigure.text: Because a fake has real behaviour, tests written against it check the *outcome* of an operation, such as the user that can now be fetched. That is more robust than checking which methods were called.

diagram.alt: A signup function connected to a repository. With the real repository it also talks to a database server, which is slow and shared. With a fake repository that stores users in a Python dictionary, everything stays in memory and private to the test.
diagram.caption: A repository backed by a database and a fake backed by a dictionary. Use the buttons to switch.

reveal.text: A fake has to copy the real store's rules, here that an id identifies a single row, for tests that use it to mean anything.

steps.headline: Test that signup sends one welcome message, using a spy in place of the mail server.

workedSteps.text: Arrange: create a spy mailer whose send method appends each message to a list called sent.
Act: call the unit with the spy passed in as the dependency, once for each new user.
Assert on what the spy recorded, which is the outcome that matters to the user: Ada was sent her message.
The spy recorded one message per signup. Work out the length of the list.

steps.headline: A test that restates the implementation breaks when the code is improved, and proves little about behaviour.

lead.text: It is tempting to double every collaborator and assert that each was called, since that seems to isolate the unit completely. The cost shows in the figure. A refactor renames an internal helper and the output stays the same. A test that checks the output stays green, but a test that asserts the helper was called fails, although nothing visible changed. This habit is called **over-mocking**, and it makes a suite that fails whenever the code is tidied.

A test of calls also proves little. It shows that the code does what the test says it does, and nothing about whether the result is right, since a unit that calls its helpers perfectly can still return the wrong answer. Checking the result, with a fake or a stub supplying the dependencies, keeps the test about behaviour and leaves the implementation free to change.

afterFigure.text: Interaction checks have their place when the call *is* the behaviour, as when a message must be sent to a customer exactly once. Elsewhere, prefer the cheapest double that lets you check the result.

diagram.alt: A refactor renames an internal helper without changing the output. A test that asserts the output stays green. A test that asserts the helper was called fails although nothing visible changed.

lead.text: A suite has 500 tests that each call a real network service for 400 ms, and each takes 2 ms once the service is replaced by a stub. Work out the effect on the whole suite.

reveal.text: Isolation pays twice: the suite runs faster, and it no longer fails when the network does.

lessons.orientation: Replace a slow or unpredictable dependency with a double and know which kind to use.
lessons.nextAction: Find inputs by properties and exploration instead of by single examples.

blocks.text: The greeting function in the figure reads the real clock, so a test that asserts 'Good morning' passes in the morning and fails in the afternoon. The same is true of any code that depends on the network, a database or a random number generator: the test cannot control what the code reads, so its result can change without the code changing.

The remedy is to make each such dependency something the test can supply. Once it is an argument, what is passed in can be anything from a fixed value to a small working replacement, and the choice among them determines how well the test survives later changes to the code.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to pass a dependency in as an argument, choose between a stub, a fake, a mock and a spy, and say why asserting internal calls makes tests brittle.
intro.whyItMatters: Tests that control their dependencies are fast, repeatable and still pass when the code is refactored.

recap.keyIdea: Pass dependencies in, replace them with the simplest double that lets you check the result, and avoid asserting how the code works inside.

blocks.text: Dependency injection hands a unit its clock, network or store as arguments, so a test can choose them. A stub supplies answers, a fake is a small working copy, a mock checks calls and a spy records them, and preferring results over calls keeps a suite from breaking whenever the code is refactored.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson goes beyond single examples, with properties that must hold for every input and generators that look for counter-examples.

lessons.title: Properties, fuzzing and exploratory testing

lead.text: A faulty sort, my_sort(xs), returns sorted(set(xs)). Its only test is my_sort([3, 1, 2]) == [1, 2, 3], which passes. Before reading on, decide what my_sort([2, 1, 2]) returns, and how long its result is.

reveal.text: The faulty function loses an item and the one example never noticed. The next screen asks what the test should have claimed instead.

steps.headline: A property is a statement that holds for every valid input, and it can be checked on any input you like.

lead.text: A test of one example says that for this input the output is that. For a sort function there is a stronger kind of claim, which holds for *every* list. The output is ordered, so that each item is at most the next. It has the same length as the input, and the same items. Sorting the output again changes nothing. Each of these is a **property**, and none of them mentions a particular list, so each can be checked on any list at all.

The first view of the figure lists the four. In the second view the faulty sort is run on [2, 1, 2] and returns [1, 2]: the output is still ordered, and still unchanged by a second sort, but it has lost an item, so two of the four properties fail. A property found the fault that the example test missed, and it would have found it on any list that contains a repeated value.

afterFigure.text: Writing a property takes more thought than writing an example, because you must say what is true of *all* the outputs, without computing a particular one. That also means a property does not need an oracle for each input, which lightens the problem described in the first lesson.

diagram.alt: Four properties of a sort function: the output is ordered, has the same length as the input, has the same items, and sorting twice equals sorting once. A second view shows a faulty sort that drops duplicates returning [1, 2] for [2, 1, 2], so the same-length and same-items properties fail.

lead.text: Check the idempotence property by hand: sort the list, sort the result, and compare.

reveal.text: A property that holds on one list is not shown to hold on all of them; the rest of the work is to try many lists, which a program can do.

steps.headline: A generator produces many inputs, and shrinking reduces the first failing one to the smallest that still fails.

lead.text: **Property-based testing** pairs a property with a **generator**, which produces many inputs of the right kind: lists of integers, say, of different lengths, with repeats and negatives and empty lists. The Hypothesis library for Python works this way. It runs the test on many generated inputs, and if the property is false for one, it reports that input as a counter-example.

A first failure is often cluttered. The generator may have found [5, 2, 8, 2, 9], where only the repeated 2 matters. A property-based tool therefore performs **shrinking**: it removes items and simplifies values, runs the property again after each change, and keeps the change if the failure remains. The figure steps through this, and ends on [0, 0], two equal items, from which nothing more can be removed. That is the minimal input the developer is shown.

afterFigure.text: The shrunk input is also an explanation: two equal values are enough, so the fault concerns duplicates. A developer given the original list would have had to work that out.

diagram.alt: Four stages of shrinking a failing input for the property that my_sort keeps the length. The list [5, 2, 8, 2, 9] shrinks to [2, 8, 2], then [2, 2], then the minimal [0, 0].

lead.text: Decide what any failing list for this fault must contain, and then how few items that takes.

reveal.text: The smallest failing input is as informative as the property that failed, because it shows the minimum that triggers the fault.

steps.headline: Random inputs can be replayed, and properties complement examples without replacing them.

lead.text: It may seem that random inputs make a failure impossible to repeat. They do not, because the generator is driven by a *seed*, and a tool records the seed, or the failing input itself, so that the next run starts from the same place. Hypothesis, for instance, remembers failing examples and tries them first the next time. A failure found by chance is therefore found again deliberately.

Properties do not replace example tests, for two reasons. Some code has no simple property, and an example such as a tax calculation for a given income is the clearest statement of what the code should do. And an example documents the behaviour for a reader, which a property does not. The two work together: examples pin down the cases that matter, and properties search for the ones nobody thought of.

afterFigure.text: Fuzzing is the same idea applied with less structure. A **fuzzer** feeds random or deliberately broken input to a program, often a parser, and watches for crashes and hangs. It needs no property beyond *must not fall over*, which suits code that reads data from outside, as the third figure compares.

diagram.alt: Two pipelines. In property-based testing a generator makes valid inputs, they go through the code under test and a property is checked on each output. In fuzzing a fuzzer makes random or mutated input for a parser and watches for crashes, hangs or errors.
diagram.caption: Property-based testing and fuzzing differ in what they generate and what they check. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Recall the figure with the four stages before choosing.

reveal.text: Shrinking leaves the property alone and changes only the input.

steps.headline: Write and check a property for a reverse function: reversing a list twice returns the original.

workedSteps.text: State the property without naming a list: for every list x, reversing x and then reversing the result gives x back.
Check it by hand on one list with a correct reverse. Python's slice x[::-1] reverses a list.
Now run it against a faulty reverse that drops the first item, bad_reverse(x) = x[:0:-1]. The first call turns [3, 1, 2] into [2, 1].
Apply it a second time and look at the length of the result, which the property says should be 3.

steps.headline: Exploratory testing combines learning, test design and execution, and a charter and a time box give it structure.

lead.text: Generated inputs search widely but they cannot judge whether a screen is confusing or a message is misleading. A person can. **Exploratory testing** is testing in which learning, test design and execution happen together: the tester uses what the program has just shown to decide what to try next. It is not unplanned. A session has a **charter**, a short statement of what to explore and why, such as exploring checkout with expired cards to find how errors are reported, and a **time box**, often an hour or so.

The tester takes notes as they go, and the findings, which may be bugs, questions or ideas for further tests, are reviewed afterwards. The figure sets this beside a scripted test, which fixes its steps and its expected result in advance. A script can be repeated exactly by anyone, which makes it good for regression, whereas a session finds problems that nobody thought to script.

afterFigure.text: A team uses both, because they find different things: scripts and generated tests guard what is known, and exploration looks for what is not.

diagram.alt: Two sheets. A scripted test case lists fixed steps, an expected result, an actual result and a verdict. An exploratory session sheet has a charter, a time box, notes and findings.
diagram.caption: A script is fixed in advance and an exploratory session is steered by a charter. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: A charter gives a session direction, so it can be compared with the notes after it.

lead.text: An encoder replaces each space with an underscore, and a decoder replaces each underscore with a space. The property to check is decode(encode(s)) == s. Apply it to a string that already contains an underscore.

reveal.text: A generator that produces strings with all kinds of characters would reach this input quickly, whereas an example written by hand probably avoids it.

lessons.orientation: State properties that must hold for all inputs and see how generation and exploration find what examples miss.
lessons.nextAction: Write a failing test first, make it pass, and tidy the code with the tests as a safety net.

blocks.text: A faulty sort that removes duplicates passes the test my_sort([3, 1, 2]) == [1, 2, 3], because that list has no duplicates to remove. The same function fails on [2, 1, 2], returning a list one item short, and nothing in the example test could have shown it.

A claim about all lists, such as that the output has the same length as the input, would catch the fault on any list with a repeated value. Claims of that kind can be checked with many inputs or with a person's curiosity.

diagram.alt: Four properties of a sort function: the output is ordered, has the same length as the input, has the same items, and sorting twice equals sorting once. A second view shows a faulty sort that drops duplicates returning [1, 2] for [2, 1, 2], so the same-length and same-items properties fail.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to state properties for a function, explain how generators and shrinking use them, and say what exploratory testing adds.
intro.whyItMatters: Examples check the cases you thought of, and properties and exploration look for the others.

recap.keyIdea: A property holds for every valid input, so generated inputs can test it widely, and exploration finds what neither examples nor properties were written to find.

blocks.text: A property is a claim about all inputs, which a generator checks on many and a shrinker reduces to a minimal failure, with a seed so the run can be replayed. Fuzzing applies the same idea to parsers with fewer assumptions, and exploratory testing, steered by a charter, adds human judgement.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson writes the test before the code, in a loop of red, green and refactor.

lessons.title: Test-driven development and refactoring

lead.text: Read the function fizz in the next question, which returns 'Fizz' for multiples of 3 and the number as text otherwise. Decide how many of the first fifteen results are 'Fizz' before any tests are written.

reveal.text: Fizz appears every third result, including 15. The loop that follows builds the function with tests, one small behaviour at a time.

steps.headline: Test-driven development repeats three steps: a failing test, the simplest code that passes it, and a tidy-up with the tests green.

lead.text: In **test-driven development**, usually shortened to TDD, the test comes before the code that it tests. The loop has three stages. In the *red* stage you write one small test for behaviour the code does not yet have, run it, and watch it fail. In the *green* stage you write the simplest code that makes it pass. In the *refactor* stage you improve the structure of the code while all the tests stay green. Then the loop starts again with the next test.

The word *one* matters. TDD is sometimes taken to mean writing all the tests first, but the unit of the loop is a single test and a few lines of code, perhaps a minute or two of work. Kent Beck described it in Test-Driven Development: By Example in 2002, drawing on practices from Extreme Programming. Seeing the test go red is not a formality. It is the check from the second lesson that the test is able to fail, and a test that was never seen to fail may be one that cannot.

afterFigure.text: The simplest code in the green stage can be startlingly simple, a function that returns a constant, because the test only asks for one case. The next test is what forces the code to become general.

diagram.alt: A loop of three stages. Red: write a failing test. Green: make it pass in the simplest way. Refactor: improve the design with the tests green. The loop then returns to red with the next test.
diagram.caption: The three stages of test-driven development. Use the buttons to move round the loop.

lead.text: Recall the first stage of the loop in the figure.

reveal.text: The failing test is also a statement of the behaviour wanted, written before the code exists.

steps.headline: Each new test asks for one more behaviour, and the code grows by the smallest change that satisfies it.

lead.text: The figure builds a function that returns the number as text, except that multiples of 3 give 'Fizz', multiples of 5 give 'Buzz' and multiples of 15 give 'FizzBuzz'. The first test asks for fizzbuzz(3) == 'Fizz' and fails because the function does not exist. The simplest code that passes it returns the constant 'Fizz'. That cheats, but it is honest to the test, and it makes the next test necessary.

That next test, fizzbuzz(1) == '1', fails because the constant returns 'Fizz', and passing it forces a condition on n % 3. A test for 5 adds the Buzz rule. A test for 15 is red in an interesting way: the function returns 'Fizz' because 15 is divisible by 3, so the code needs a special case, placed *first*. Each red tells you what is missing, and each green leaves a working function and a passing suite.

afterFigure.text: The order of the tests is a design decision. Choosing the next test is choosing the smallest behaviour that the code cannot yet show.

diagram.alt: Four cycles of building a function fizzbuzz. Each cycle adds one test that fails, then the smallest change to the code that makes it pass. The code grows from returning Fizz, to a test for multiples of three, then of five, then of fifteen.
diagram.caption: Four cycles, each with a failing test and the smallest code that passes. Use the buttons to move through them.

lead.text: Run the three tests in your head against the code from cycle 2, one at a time.

reveal.text: The test that fails is the one that begins the next cycle.

steps.headline: Refactoring changes the structure of code and not its behaviour, and the tests are what show that nothing changed.

lead.text: After the fourth cycle the function works but has a special case that repeats the other two rules. The figure shows a restructuring: build the result from the Fizz piece and the Buzz piece, and fall back to the number when both are empty. For 15 the two pieces join to 'FizzBuzz', so the special case is no longer needed. This kind of change is called **refactoring**: altering the structure of code without altering its behaviour.

The definition has a strict edge. If a refactoring changes any result, it is not a refactoring but a change of behaviour, and it should be a separate step with its own test. The test suite is what makes the strictness practical: you make the change, run every test, and green means that every behaviour you wrote a test for is intact. Without tests the same edit would rely on careful reading, and mistakes would be found later by users.

afterFigure.text: Refactoring belongs in the third stage, when everything is green, because a red test during a restructuring leaves you unsure whether the code or the tidy-up caused it.

diagram.alt: Two versions of fizzbuzz with the same behaviour. Before, a special case for 15 comes first. After, the Fizz and Buzz pieces are joined, so no special case for 15 is needed. In both the tests are green.

lead.text: The refactored function must produce the same results as before. Count the results for 1 to 15 that are not just the number as text.

reveal.text: The count is a check that nothing changed, and a full set of tests for these results would be run after the refactoring.

steps.headline: A bug fix begins with a test that fails because of the bug, and that test then stays as a regression test.

lead.text: A **regression** is a change that breaks behaviour that used to work, and a **regression test** is one that stops it from happening again. The cheapest way to write one is to apply the loop to the bug. Say a customer reports that a discount is applied twice: a price of 200 with 50 per cent off should total 100 but comes out lower. The first step is not to look for the fault but to write the test, assert total(200, 50) == 100, and watch it fail.

Then fix the code, and the same test turns green. Written this way the test has been seen to fail for exactly the reason in the report, so it is known to detect the bug, and it stays in the suite as a permanent guard. A test written after the fix, which passes the first time it is run, has not shown that it could have caught the bug.

afterFigure.text: A team that fixes every bug in this order accumulates a suite that grows out of real failures, and these are often the ones most likely to occur again.

diagram.alt: A four-stage timeline of fixing a bug with a regression test. A bug is reported, a test that fails is written, the fix is applied and the test passes, and the test stays in the suite.
diagram.caption: The life of a regression test. Use the buttons to move along the timeline.

steps.headline: Fix the double discount with a regression test written first.

workedSteps.text: Write the test from the bug report, with the numbers the customer saw.
Run it against the current code, which applies the discount twice. The first discount gives 100 and the second is applied to that.
Work out what the current code returns, and confirm that it differs from 100, so the test is red for the reason reported.
Remove the second discount from the function, so that total returns after, and run the test again. It now returns 100 and passes.

lead.text: Choose different numbers for the same bug, so that the regression test and the old code can be compared again: a price of 300 with 20 per cent off.

reveal.text: A regression test that fails on the old code, for any numbers, is the evidence that it will catch the bug if it returns.

lessons.orientation: Follow red, green, refactor on a small function and write a regression test before a fix.
lessons.nextAction: Place tests at the unit, integration and end-to-end levels by cost and speed.

blocks.text: A function fizz returns 'Fizz' for multiples of 3 and the number as text otherwise, and the simplest way to produce it is to write the code and then add tests. Test-driven development reverses that order: each test is written first, seen to fail, and only then satisfied by the least code that passes it.

The reversal has a consequence for the whole suite. Every test has been seen to fail for the reason it names, and the code has been grown only as far as a test asked, so that code and tests arrive together and stay in step.

diagram.alt: A loop of three stages. Red: write a failing test. Green: make it pass in the simplest way. Refactor: improve the design with the tests green. The loop then returns to red with the next test.
diagram.caption: The three stages of test-driven development. Use the buttons to move round the loop.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to follow red, green, refactor on a small function and write a failing test before a bug fix.
intro.whyItMatters: A loop of small steps with a safety net lets you change code without fearing what it breaks.

recap.keyIdea: Write a failing test, make it pass with the simplest code, then refactor with the tests green, and begin every bug fix with a test that fails.

blocks.text: The loop of red, green and refactor builds a function one tested behaviour at a time, and the tests are what make refactoring safe. A regression test written from a bug report fails before the fix and passes after it, which keeps the bug from coming back.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson places tests at the unit, integration and end-to-end levels and asks what each costs.

lessons.title: Test levels and the pyramid

lead.text: Suite A has 1,000 unit tests of 5 ms each, and suite B has only 50 end-to-end tests of 20 s each. Before reading on, decide how many times longer suite B takes than suite A.

reveal.text: Fifty tests take two hundred times as long as a thousand. The next screens say why the levels differ so much.

steps.headline: Tests sit at three levels according to how much of the system they exercise: unit, integration and end to end.

lead.text: A **unit test** exercises one piece alone, such as the order logic in the figure, with whatever it depends on replaced by a double. It is fast, which is why a suite can hold thousands, and a failure names the piece. An **integration test** exercises several pieces together, such as the order logic with a real database, to check that they agree about how they are connected. It costs more to set up and run, and a failure points at the connection.

An **end-to-end test** drives a whole user journey through the real system, from the interface to the data store. It is the most realistic, since it checks what a user would see, and it is also the slowest and the least specific: a failure says only that something along the journey broke. The levels are a scale and not three sharp categories, and the useful question about a test is how much of the system it needs in order to run.

afterFigure.text: The levels catch different faults. A unit test cannot find a mismatch between two pieces, and an end-to-end test can find one but will take a long time to say where it is.

diagram.alt: Three boxes in a row: UI, order logic and database. A unit test covers only the order logic. An integration test covers the order logic and the database. An end-to-end test covers all three.
