lead.text: Name the kind of test that runs from the interface to the data store.

reveal.text: The more of the system a test needs, the more it costs to run, and the next screen turns this into a shape.

steps.headline: A healthy suite has many fast low-level tests and few slow high-level ones, in the shape of a pyramid.

lead.text: Cost and speed push the number of tests at each level in a direction. Unit tests are cheap, so many can be written and run on every change. End-to-end tests are expensive, so each must justify itself. Drawn with width for number of tests, the result is a **test pyramid**, with unit tests as the base, integration tests above and a few end-to-end tests at the top. The picture was popularised by Mike Cohn, and the Practical Test Pyramid article on martinfowler.com explains how to apply it.

Arithmetic shows why. A thousand unit tests at 5 ms take 5 seconds, a time nobody minds waiting for. Fifty end-to-end tests at 20 seconds take 1,000 seconds, about 16.7 minutes, and a suite that slow is run less often, so mistakes are found later. The second view inverts the shape. A team that tests mainly through the interface has a suite that is slow, whose failures are far from their cause, and which often fails for reasons unrelated to the code.

afterFigure.text: The shape is a guide and not a rule. What it says is to test each behaviour at the lowest level that can show it.

reveal.text: That is the cost of one run, and it is paid again each time the suite is run.

steps.headline: A flaky test sometimes fails on the same code, and across a large suite even a small rate makes a false failure likely.

lead.text: A **flaky** test is one that passes on some runs and fails on others without any change to the code. Each flaky failure is rare, so it seems harmless, but the chances add up across a suite. If each of 50 independent tests has a 1% chance of a false failure, the chance that all 50 pass is 0.99 multiplied by itself 50 times, which is 0.605. The chance of at least one false failure is therefore 1 − 0.605 = 0.395, or about 39.5%. Two runs in five would be red for no reason.

The figure shows how the chance grows with the suite, for three failure rates. The cost is more than the wasted time. When red results are often false, people learn to rerun and ignore them, and the red that signals a real defect goes unnoticed. A flaky test that passes tells you nothing, and one that fails tells you little.

afterFigure.text: Rerunning until green is therefore not a remedy. It removes the visible failure and keeps the cause, and the suite's information is lost.

steps.headline: Work out the chance that a run of 50 tests has at least one false failure, when each test has a 1% chance.

workedSteps.text: Each test passes with probability 0.99, since it fails falsely 1% of the time.
The tests are independent, so the chance that all 50 pass is the product of 50 factors of 0.99.
At least one failure is the opposite of every test passing, so subtract from 1.
Write the chance as a percentage, to one decimal place.

lead.text: Apply the same method to a larger suite of 100 independent tests with the same 1% flake rate.

reveal.text: The chance of a false red grows with the suite even though no individual test got worse.

steps.headline: Flakiness has a few usual causes, and each has a remedy that gives the test control of what varied.

lead.text: Most flaky tests depend on something that varies and that the test does not control. A fixed sleep, such as waiting two seconds for a page to load, fails on a slow day. Shared data lets one test change what another reads, and a test that passes only after another test has run depends on the order. The real clock and the network add variation of their own, as the lesson on test doubles showed.

Each cause has a remedy that gives the control back to the test. Wait for a condition to hold, with a timeout, instead of for a fixed time. Have each test create its own data, and set up what it needs instead of relying on a predecessor. Inject a stand-in for the clock or the network. A test that cannot be fixed at once can be *quarantined*, which means taking it out of the blocking suite while keeping it visible, and repaired within a set time.

afterFigure.text: The test levels also help here. End-to-end tests have the most moving parts, and so they are flaky most often, which is another reason to keep them few.

lead.text: Name a test that gives different results on different runs of the same code.

reveal.text: The name describes unreliable results, whatever the cause, and not a test that fails consistently.

lead.text: A team replaces 20 of its 50 end-to-end tests, at 20 s each, with 20 unit tests of 5 ms each that check the same logic. Work out the effect on the run time, in seconds.

reveal.text: Moving a check down the pyramid saves its time and shortens the path from a failure to its cause.

lessons.orientation: Place tests at unit, integration and end-to-end levels by cost and speed, and compute the effect of flakiness.
lessons.nextAction: Test a query and a data set with checks, and use contract tests at service boundaries.

blocks.text: Two suites can have the same purpose and very different costs. A thousand unit tests at 5 ms each finish in 5 seconds, and fifty end-to-end tests at 20 seconds each take 1,000 seconds, about 16.7 minutes. Which level a test sits at decides how often it can be run, how quickly it reports and how specific the report is.

The same decision affects reliability. A test with many moving parts is more likely to fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the code, and that unreliability adds up over a suite in a way that a single test's rate hides.

diagram.alt: A pyramid of three layers with unit tests as the wide base, integration tests in the middle and a few end-to-end tests at the top. The second view inverts it, with many end-to-end tests at the top and few unit tests at the base.
diagram.caption: The same three levels with the weight in different places. Use the buttons to compare.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place tests at the right level by cost and speed, and compute how flakiness affects a run.
intro.whyItMatters: A suite that is fast and trustworthy is run constantly, and one that is slow or flaky stops being used.

recap.keyIdea: Test each behaviour at the lowest level that can show it, keep the slow levels few, and treat flakiness as damage to the suite's information.

blocks.text: Unit tests are fast and specific, integration tests check connections and end-to-end tests check a whole journey slowly, so a healthy suite is a pyramid. Flakiness compounds across a suite, giving a false failure in about two runs in five at 1% for each of 50 tests, so a flaky test must be fixed and not rerun.

lessons.title: Testing data, queries and APIs

lead.text: A customers table has four rows with the emails a@x, b@x, a@x and c@x, and the rule is that each email appears once. Work out how many rows would have to be removed to satisfy it.

reveal.text: The count of surplus rows is simple here, and the next screen shows how a query finds duplicates in a table with a million rows.

steps.headline: A data quality check is a query that returns the rows that break a rule, so an empty result means the data passes.

lead.text: Tests are not limited to code. A table can be wrong in ways that no program is at fault for, such as two customers with the same email, a missing value, or an amount outside its range. A **data quality check** is a query written to find such rows. The convention is that it returns the *violations*, so that an empty result passes and any row returned is a fault to inspect.

The figure's second view shows the check for the rule that each email appears once. Grouping rows by email and keeping the groups with more than one row returns a single row, a@x with a count of 2. Other common rules are written the same way: a not-null check returns rows where a column IS NULL, a range check returns rows with an amount below zero, and a reference check returns orders whose customer id has no matching customer.

afterFigure.text: A shorter form counts the surplus rows, COUNT(*) − COUNT(DISTINCT email), which is zero when every email is unique. For the four rows above it is 4 − 3 = 1.

diagram.alt: A customers table with four rows and the emails a@x, b@x, a@x and c@x. In a second view a check query groups by email and keeps groups larger than one, and returns a single row, a@x with count 2, which marks the violation.
diagram.caption: A table with a duplicate email, and the check that finds it. Use the buttons to run the check.

steps.headline: An API test checks the status, the shape of the response, the error cases and what happens when a request is repeated.

lead.text: A service's API is the set of requests that other programs may send, and testing it directly is quicker and more precise than testing it through a user interface that also uses it. For each request an **API test** asserts several things. The *status code* says whether the call succeeded, for instance 200 for a found order and 404 for one that does not exist. The *shape* of the body says which fields are present and of what type. The *error cases* check that a bad request gets a clear error and changes nothing.

A fourth check concerns repetition. A request is **idempotent** when sending it several times leaves the system in the same state as sending it once. Setting an order's status to paid with PUT is idempotent, and creating an order with POST is not, because each success adds another. Clients retry when a reply is lost, so a test that sends the request twice and compares the state is one of the more valuable tests an API can have.

afterFigure.text: A user-interface test that passes does not show that the API is right, since the interface may be hiding the error. The API deserves tests of its own.

diagram.alt: Three API exchanges and what a test asserts for each. A successful GET returns 200 with a body that has an id and a total. A GET for a missing order returns 404 with an error message. Repeating the same PUT leaves the order in the same state as sending it once.
diagram.caption: What an API test checks: status, shape, errors and repeated requests. Use the buttons to compare three exchanges.

reveal.text: The retries are harmless only for requests that are idempotent, and POST is not one unless it carries an idempotency key.

steps.headline: A contract test checks that a provider and a consumer agree on the shape and meaning of the messages between them.

lead.text: Services built by different teams depend on each other's messages. The consumer reads a field called total, and the provider decides to rename it to amount. Each team's own tests still pass, because the consumer's tests use a stand-in for the provider and the provider's tests know nothing of the consumer. The break appears only when the two are connected in production.

A **contract test** closes the gap. The consumer states what it relies on, the field total as a number, and that statement is the contract. The provider runs the contract against its real responses in its own build. In the figure's second view the provider renames the field, the contract test fails at once, and it fails in the build of the team that made the change, before release. Contracts written by the consumers are called *consumer-driven*, and they let each side change freely as long as the contract holds.

afterFigure.text: A contract test is small and fast, since it checks the shape of messages and not whole journeys, so it sits well below the end-to-end level of the pyramid.

diagram.alt: A consumer, a contract and a provider. The contract says the response has a numeric field called total. In the first view the provider returns total and the contract test passes. In the second the provider renames the field to amount, and the contract test fails in the provider's build.
diagram.caption: A contract between a consumer and a provider. Use the buttons to rename the field.

lead.text: Pick the test that compares what a consumer relies on with what the provider now returns.

reveal.text: Contracts are the cheapest way to find a break between services before it is released.

steps.headline: Each test should create the small, deliberate data it needs, and leave shared state and production copies alone.

lead.text: A test needs data, and where it comes from affects whether the test can be trusted. A copy of production data seems realistic, but it may contain personal information that tests should not hold, and it hides the case under test among millions of rows. A shared database causes the problem in the figure: test B passes if test A ran before it and fails if not, so its result depends on the order.

The remedy is for each test to create exactly the rows it needs. A *builder* function makes this cheap: customer(email='a@x') returns a valid customer with sensible defaults for every field the test does not care about, so that the test names only the detail that matters. The data is small, the test says what it assumes, and the order of tests no longer matters.

afterFigure.text: Data built per test is also the easiest to read. The reader sees the customer with a duplicate email in the test itself, not in a fixture file elsewhere.

diagram.alt: Two tests, A and B, run in two orders. When they share one database, the result of test B depends on whether test A ran first. When each test builds its own data, both pass in either order.

workedSteps.text: The data has four rows. Group them by email, which gives one group for each different address.

workedSteps.text: Keep only the groups that have more than one row, which is the HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 part of the query.
The query returns one row for each group that was kept. Work out how many rows the check returns.
The check returned a row, so the data does not meet the rule. Fix the data or the code that wrote it, and run the check again until it returns nothing.

lead.text: A different request type now: a client sends the same PUT three times and compares the state with the state after one.

reveal.text: Repeated-request tests are a short way to find handlers that quietly assume each request arrives only once.

blocks.text: A customers table with the emails a@x, b@x, a@x and c@x breaks a rule that no program is at fault for: two rows share an address. A query that groups by email and keeps the groups larger than one returns the violation, and a table that obeys the rule returns nothing.

The same approach reaches the interfaces between programs. A request to a service can be tested for its status, its fields and its behaviour when it is repeated, and the agreement between two services can itself be written as a test that fails when one side changes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a SQL check that finds rule violations, say what an API test asserts, and explain how a contract test catches a breaking change.
intro.whyItMatters: Data and interfaces break in ways that unit tests of code never see, and these tests find them cheaply.

recap.keyIdea: A check query returns the rows that break a rule, an API test asserts status, shape, errors and repeats, and a contract test catches a break between services before release.

blocks.text: Data quality checks return violations, so an empty result passes. API tests assert status, shape, errors and idempotence, and a contract test lets a provider find out in its own build that a change would break a consumer, provided every test builds the data it needs.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to how fast and how reliably the software runs, with percentiles, Little's law and load tests.

lessons.title: Performance and other non-functional tests

lead.text: The twenty response times of a service are drawn in the next figure, ranging from 12 ms to 450 ms. Work out their mean, and then count how many of the twenty requests were slower than that mean.

reveal.text: Only three requests are slower than the mean, which says something about how well a mean describes the users of this service.

steps.headline: A percentile is a value that a given share of the observations does not exceed, and it shows the slow tail that the mean hides.

lead.text: The mean of the twenty times is 48.8 ms, a number that no typical request resembles. Seventeen requests took 41 ms or less, and three took 58, 120 and 450 ms. The mean is pulled up by the slowest request, so it lies above most of the data and says little about either the typical request or the unlucky one.

A **percentile** describes the tail directly. The *p*-th percentile is a value such that *p* per cent of the observations are at or below it. One simple definition, the **nearest rank** method, takes the rank ceil(*p*/100 × *n*) in the sorted list, where *n* is the number of values and ceil rounds up. For the twenty times the 50th percentile has rank 10, which is 19 ms, the 90th has rank 18, which is 58 ms, and the 95th has rank 19, which is 120 ms. The second view of the figure marks all three beside the mean.

afterFigure.text: A statement such as *95 per cent of requests finish within 120 ms* tells a user what to expect and tells a team what to improve. Performance targets are therefore usually written as percentiles. Other definitions of the percentile interpolate between values, and the figures differ slightly.

steps.headline: Little's law says that the average number of requests in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there.

lead.text: A different question is how many requests are being handled at the same moment, which decides how many threads, connections or machines are needed. **Little's law** answers it. If requests arrive at an average rate λ per second and each spends an average time W seconds in the system, then the average number in the system, written L, is L = λ × W. The figure's first view has 200 requests arriving each second and each taking 0.25 s, so 200 × 0.25 = 50 requests are in flight at any moment.

The law was proved by John Little in 1961, and it holds for any stable system whatever the pattern of arrivals, which is why it is so useful. The second view doubles the time to 0.5 s and the number in flight doubles to 100. This is the usual way for a slow dependency to exhaust a connection pool: nothing about the arrival rate changed, but each request now stays longer, and more of them are inside at once.

afterFigure.text: The law connects a test result to a capacity decision. A load test reports W at a given λ, and L is the number of slots the system must provide for that load.

lead.text: Use the law on a new service, being careful to multiply the rate by the time and not to divide.

reveal.text: The result is the number of slots a pool needs, on average, and peaks need more.

steps.headline: Load, stress and soak tests ask different questions of the same system, and each has an expected demand to compare with.

lead.text: Performance tests apply demand to a running system and measure what happens, and they differ in how much demand and for how long. A **load test** applies the demand that is expected and checks the targets, such as a 95th-percentile time under 300 ms. A **stress test** goes beyond the expected demand, to find the **breaking point**, the load at which the system fails or its response time climbs steeply, and to see *how* it fails: whether it slows, refuses requests or crashes.

Two more kinds are common. A **soak test** holds a normal load for hours to find faults that grow slowly, such as a memory leak, and a **spike test** raises the load suddenly to see whether the system recovers. The curve in the figure is typical, flat for a while and then rising steeply, and each test looks at a different part of it. Without a stated expected demand, a load test has nothing to compare with, so the expected demand is the first number to write down.

afterFigure.text: All of these report in percentiles, not means, and they are best run against something like production, since a test machine with a different size gives different results.

diagram.alt: A curve of latency against load that stays low and then climbs steeply. A load test covers loads up to the expected demand. A stress test continues beyond it to the breaking point. A soak test holds the expected demand for many hours to look for slow decay.
diagram.caption: What load, stress and soak tests each ask of the same system. Use the buttons to compare them.

lead.text: Recall which of the tests in the figure goes past the expected demand.

reveal.text: A system that fails gracefully under stress is often worth more than one that is slightly faster.

steps.headline: Non-functional tests are judged against thresholds and checklists, and tools find only part of what they look for.

lead.text: Performance is one of several qualities beyond *what* the software does, together called **non-functional** and tested in their own way. A functional test has an exact expected result, whereas most of these are judged against a threshold or a checklist: the 95th percentile must be under 300 ms, the error rate must stay under a stated figure, the site must meet a chosen accessibility standard. Figures for how each is judged appear in the second view.

Security testing looks for ways that the software can be abused, and the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide organises that work as a set of checks. Accessibility testing asks whether people who use screen readers, keyboards alone or magnification can use the product. Both are partly automated, and in both an automated tool detects only a part of the problems, so a clean report from a tool means that nothing it can detect was found, and manual testing by people covers the rest.

afterFigure.text: Because the pass condition is a threshold, the threshold has to be chosen before the test, from what users need. A threshold written after seeing the result is a description of the result.

diagram.alt: Four kinds of non-functional test with the question each asks and a typical pass rule. Performance asks whether it is fast enough, security whether it can be abused, accessibility whether everyone can use it, and reliability whether it keeps working.
diagram.caption: Four non-functional tests, with what each asks and how it is judged. Use the buttons to switch.

lead.text: Decide what a clean report from an automated accessibility tool can and cannot show.

reveal.text: Tools are good at catching what is mechanical, such as missing text alternatives, and weaker at judging whether a page makes sense to someone using it.

lead.text: Ten response times in ms, sorted, are 100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150, 160, 170, 180 and 900. Use the same method on this new list to find the 90th percentile.

reveal.text: With ten values the rank for the 90th percentile is 9, so the single outlier at rank 10 is excluded, and it takes the 100th percentile to reach it.

lessons.orientation: Read percentiles, apply Little's law, and say what load, stress and accessibility tests each answer.
lessons.nextAction: Write a useful bug report, compute defect detection effectiveness, and place tests in a delivery pipeline.

blocks.text: Twenty response times of a service range from 12 ms to 450 ms, and their mean is 48.8 ms, which is larger than seventeen of them. A figure that sits above most of the data is a poor summary, and a team that reports it would miss the three users who waited longer than 58 ms.

Performance work therefore uses percentiles, which describe the slow tail directly, and a small amount of queueing arithmetic to turn a response time into a capacity. The same ideas extend to the other qualities of software that cannot be tested with an exact expected value.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the mean and nearest-rank percentiles, apply Little's law, and say what load, stress and soak tests each ask.
intro.whyItMatters: Performance claims are only useful when they are stated as percentiles at a stated load.

recap.keyIdea: Describe response times with percentiles, size capacity with Little's law, and judge non-functional qualities against thresholds chosen in advance.

blocks.text: The mean hides a slow tail that percentiles show, and nearest rank picks the value at rank ceil(p/100 × n). Little's law turns an arrival rate and a time into the requests in flight, and load, stress and soak tests ask different questions of the same system against a stated expected demand.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson turns to defects themselves: how to report one, how to count what testing found, and where tests sit in a delivery pipeline.

lessons.title: Defects, quality measures and testing in delivery

steps.headline: A useful bug report lets someone else make the fault happen again, with the steps, the expected and actual results, the environment and the evidence.

lead.text: A defect found by a tester is of no use until someone can fix it, and someone else must usually do it. The first view of the figure is a report that fails at this. It says that checkout is broken and gives the reader nothing to follow: no steps, no statement of what should have happened, no version, no evidence. The developer's first response will be a question, and often the report waits days for an answer.

The second view reports the same fault so that it can be acted on. A short title says what failed and when, the *steps to reproduce* are numbered, the *expected* and *actual* results are separate, so the fault is a stated disagreement and not an opinion, and the environment and evidence are attached. Of these the steps matter most, since a fault that can be reproduced can be investigated, and one that cannot is usually closed.

afterFigure.text: A good report also stays on the fault. Guesses about the cause belong in a comment, because a wrong guess in the title sends the investigation the wrong way.

diagram.alt: Two bug reports. The weak one says it is broken and asks for a fix, with no steps, expected result, environment or evidence. The useful one lists a title, steps to reproduce, the expected and actual results, the environment and evidence.
diagram.caption: A weak and a useful report of the same fault. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Think about what a developer needs before any investigation can begin.

reveal.text: The other elements help, and the steps make the rest possible.

steps.headline: Severity is the impact of a defect, priority is the order in which it should be fixed, and the two can differ.

lead.text: Two words are often used for the same thing, though they mean different things. **Severity** is the impact of a defect on users and on the product: how much harm it does. **Priority** is the order in which defects should be fixed, and it depends on impact together with other things, such as how many people see it, how visible it is, and what else is waiting.

The grid in the figure gives four examples. A crash in an admin report that is rarely opened is *high* in severity, since the program fails, and *low* in priority, because almost nobody meets it. A company name misspelt on the landing page does no harm to anyone's work, so its severity is *low*, but every visitor sees it and the fix takes a minute, so its priority is *high*. Payments failing for everyone is high on both. Keeping the two fields separate stops the team from arguing about one word with two meanings.

afterFigure.text: Severity is usually set by the tester or reporter, who knows the impact, and priority by the person who owns the plan, who knows what else competes for time.

diagram.alt: A grid of severity against priority with four example defects. A crash in a rarely used admin report is high severity and low priority. Card payments failing for everyone is high on both. A misaligned icon is low on both. A misspelt company name on the landing page is low severity and high priority.

lead.text: Choose the word for the harm that a defect causes, as opposed to the urgency of fixing it.

reveal.text: The second word in the pair is the one that sets the queue.

lead.text: A team found 45 defects before release, and users reported 5 more after release. Before the next screen names a measure, work out what share of the defects found overall the team found before release.

reveal.text: The share is a measure of how well testing did against what users eventually found, and the next screen gives it a name.

steps.headline: Defect detection percentage compares what testing found before release with all that was found, and it must be read with care.

lead.text: The share in the figure is called the **defect detection percentage**, often abbreviated DDP: the defects found before release, divided by those found before and after release together. Team A found 45 before and 5 after, so its DDP is 45 ÷ 50 = 90%. Team B found 30 before and 20 after, which gives 30 ÷ 50 = 60%, and users met many more of its defects.

The figure comes with two cautions. The count after release grows for months, since users keep finding defects, so a DDP measured early is flattering and one measured later falls. And a count of defects found is not a measure of quality in itself: a team that finds many defects may have worse code or better testing, and the number cannot say which. The measure is a prompt for questions, such as *where do the late defects come from*, and the answers show where testing is thin.

afterFigure.text: The numbers can still be used to compare releases of the same product, for which the cautions mostly cancel out.

lead.text: Apply the same calculation to Team B.

reveal.text: Team B's late defects are the ones to examine: each shows a kind of test that was missing.

steps.headline: Testing works best at both ends of delivery, early to find defects cheaply and after release to find what earlier tests missed.

lead.text: A delivery pipeline runs a change through stages, and the figure puts a kind of test at each. Fast unit tests and a code review run at commit. Integration and contract tests run when changes are merged, and end-to-end and performance tests run in a staging environment that resembles production. The last stage is production itself. Moving checks to the start of this line is called **shifting left**, because a defect found while it is still a requirement or a line of code is cheaper to repair than one found after release.

Not every defect can be found before release, since real traffic has variety that no test set matches. **Shifting right** means observing the software in use. Monitoring shows errors and slow requests as they happen, and a **canary release** sends a new version to a small share of users first so that a problem affects few. The DORA research uses a measure of this, the *change failure rate*, the share of deployments that need a fix or a rollback, which a team reads together with how quickly service is restored.

afterFigure.text: Neither end is enough alone. Testing early cannot predict production, and observing only after release lets the users find every fault.

diagram.alt: A delivery pipeline with four stages: commit with unit tests and review, merge with integration and contract tests, staging with end-to-end and performance tests, and production with monitoring and canary releases. One view highlights the early stages, called shifting left, and the other highlights production, called shifting right.
diagram.caption: Where tests and observation sit in delivery. Use the buttons to compare shifting left with shifting right.

lead.text: Name the practice that limits the damage of a faulty release by exposing it to few users first.

reveal.text: The practice needs monitoring to be useful, since the small group's experience is the evidence.

steps.headline: Rank four areas of a product by risk, to decide where to spend testing effort first.

workedSteps.text: Give each area a likelihood of failure and an impact of failure, each from 1 to 5. Payments score 2 and 5, login 3 and 4, search 4 and 2, and the colour theme 4 and 1.
Multiply likelihood by impact for each area to get a risk score.
Order the areas from the highest score to the lowest.
Test the area at the top first and in the most depth. Read off the highest score.

lead.text: A team made 80 deployments in a month, and 6 of them needed a fix or a rollback. Work out its change failure rate.

reveal.text: The measure applies the same division as the defect detection percentage, with the failed deployments as the part and all deployments as the whole.

lessons.nextAction: Use the whole course to decide what to test, at which level, and how far to trust the result.

blocks.text: A team that found 45 defects before release and had 5 more reported by users afterwards found 90% of the defects that anyone found. The figure is useful because it ties a team's testing to what users eventually met, and it needs a careful reading, since the count of defects after release keeps growing for months.

Defects also have to be reported, ranked and placed in the delivery of the software. Practical parts of testing remain: the report that someone else can act on, the two separate judgements of severity and priority, and the stages of a pipeline in which each kind of test belongs.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a reproducible bug report, tell severity from priority, compute defect detection percentage, and place tests in a pipeline.
intro.whyItMatters: These practices decide whether what testing finds is acted on, and whether the figures are read fairly.

recap.keyIdea: A report with steps lets a fault be fixed, severity and priority are different judgements, and detection percentage and early and late testing show how well a team's testing is working.

blocks.text: Severity is the impact of a defect and priority the order of fixing, and a report that someone can reproduce gets fixed. Defect detection percentage compares defects found before release with all found, and testing is spread along the pipeline, early to find defects cheaply and after release by monitoring and canaries, with the most effort placed where failure costs most.

questions.prompt: Add the test is_leap(1900) is False to the five tests in the figure. The function is year % 4 == 0. How many of the six tests pass?
hints: Work out 1900 % 4 and decide what the function returns.
Compare that with the expected value, False.
A test passes only when the actual result equals the expected result; count the other five too.
questions.onCorrect: The sixth test fails because 1900 is divisible by 4 but is a century not divisible by 400; the five earlier tests never tried such a year.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first five inputs behave as expected. For 1900 the function returns True because 1900 % 4 == 0, but the expected value is False, so that test fails: 5 pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the sixth test as passing. 1900 % 4 is 0, so the function returns True, and the expected value is False.
The five earlier tests still pass. Only the sixth is affected.

questions.prompt: A new sorting function is checked by comparing its output with the output of Python's built-in sorted on the same list. What is the built-in sorted serving as in this test?
hints: The word names where the expected result comes from.
questions.onCorrect: An oracle supplies the expected result and must be more trustworthy than the code being tested.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the oracle: the source of the expected result.

misconceptions.feedback: An assertion is the line that compares the two results. The thing it compares against has its own name.
A mock replaces a dependency of the code under test. Here the built-in provides the expected answer.

questions.prompt: A calculator app matches every line of its specification, but the people who use it wanted to enter fractions, and the specification never mentioned them. Which check would have caught the problem?
hints: Does the product match the specification, or the need?
Which check compares the product with what users want?
questions.onCorrect: Validation compares the product with what users need; a product can pass verification and still fail it.

choices.label: A unit test of each function

misconceptions.feedback: Verification would pass, because the product does match its specification. The specification itself is what is wrong.
Unit tests check the code against what the specification says, so they would pass too.
Static analysis examines the source for defects of form and does not compare the product with what users need.

questions.prompt: A function takes two 32-bit integers. How many input pairs are there, written as a power of two? Give the exponent.
hints: Count the values one integer can take.
Multiply the counts for the two integers, and add the exponents.
questions.onCorrect: Exponents add when powers of two are multiplied, so 2^32 × 2^32 = 2^64, about 1.8 × 10^19 pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each integer has 2^32 values, so pairs number 2^32 × 2^32 = 2^64.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for one integer. A pair multiplies the counts: 2^32 × 2^32.
Multiplying exponents gives 32 × 32; when powers of the same base are multiplied the exponents add.
Two is the number of arguments. Each argument has 2^32 values.

questions.prompt: Checking all 2^64 pairs at a billion tests a second takes how many years? Use 365.25 days in a year and give the nearest whole number.
hints: First find the number of seconds: divide the number of tests by the rate.
Then divide the seconds by the seconds in a year, 365.25 × 24 × 3600.
About 31.6 million seconds make a year.
questions.onCorrect: At a billion tests a second the run would take about 585 years, which is why exhaustive testing is out of reach for even a two-argument function.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2^64 ≈ 1.8447 × 10^19 tests at 10^9 a second is 1.8447 × 10^10 seconds. A year of 365.25 days has 31,557,600 seconds, and 1.8447 × 10^10 ÷ 31,557,600 ≈ 584.5, which rounds to 585.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of seconds, about 1.84 × 10^10. Divide by the seconds in a year.

questions.prompt: Why does the working divide 2^64 by 10^9?
hints: Tests divided by tests per second leaves what unit?
questions.onCorrect: Dividing a count by a rate gives a time.

choices.label: Because 10^9 tests a second is the rate, so dividing the test count by it gives seconds.
Because 10^9 is the number of bits in an integer.
Because the result should be a power of two.
Because the tests run in parallel.

acceptedIdeas: Because 10^9 tests a second is the rate, so dividing the test count by it gives seconds.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Because 10^9 tests a second is the rate, so dividing the test count by it gives seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: An integer here has 32 bits. The 10^9 is the number of tests that can be run each second.
The division produces a time in seconds, not a power of two.
The rate already counts tests per second; nothing in the working assumes parallel runs.

questions.prompt: A function takes two 12-bit integers. How many input pairs are there in total?
hints: How many values can one 12-bit integer take?
Multiply the counts for the two integers.
questions.onCorrect: Even at 12 bits there are over sixteen million pairs; the count squares each time a second argument is added.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each integer has 2^12 = 4,096 values, so pairs number 4,096 × 4,096 = 2^24 = 16,777,216.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for one integer. A pair needs 4,096 × 4,096.
24 is the exponent. The question asks for the number of pairs, 2^24.

questions.prompt: Testing can show that defects are present, but it cannot show their what?
hints: The word is the opposite of presence.
questions.onCorrect: A suite can only report on the inputs it tried, so a pass never shows that no input would fail.

questions.prompt: Before any code exists, a team reads the requirements for a booking system and finds two rules that contradict each other. What name is given to checking that finds defects without running a program?
hints: The word describes checks that do not execute the code.
It is the opposite of dynamic testing.
questions.onCorrect: Reviews are static testing: they find defects in documents and code without running them.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Static testing, which includes reviews of documents and code.

misconceptions.feedback: Dynamic testing runs the program. Here nothing has been written yet.

questions.prompt: A team builds a form exactly as its specification describes, and every test against the specification passes, but the form asks for information that the people filling it in do not have. Which check failed?
hints: Which comparison involves the users' need?
questions.onCorrect: A product that matches its specification can still fail validation when the specification asks for the wrong thing.

misconceptions.feedback: Verification compared the form with its specification, and that comparison passed.
The unit tests used the specification as their oracle, so they passed with it.
A regression suite checks that earlier behaviour still holds, which is not in question here.

hints: The condition 2 + 2 == 5 is false.
What does the text after the comma become when the assertion fails?
questions.onCorrect: A failed assert raises AssertionError carrying the message, and the except clause printed that message.

misconceptions.feedback: AssertionError is the type of the exception. print(e) shows the message it carries.
The code prints the message, not a truth value; and 2 + 2 == 5 is false.

questions.prompt: These four tests are run against the broken function is_leap(year) = year % 4 == 0. The tests expect: 1900 gives False, 2000 gives True, 2100 gives False, 2023 gives False. How many of the four fail?
hints: Work out the function's result for each year, then compare it with the expected value.
1900 % 4 and 2100 % 4 are both 0.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Both failing years are centuries that 400 does not divide, which are the inputs that distinguish the correct rule from the broken one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The broken function returns True for 1900 and 2100 because both are divisible by 4, so those two tests fail. It returns True for 2000 and False for 2023, as expected: 2 fail.

misconceptions.feedback: 2000 and 2023 give the expected answers with this function, so those two pass.
2100 behaves like 1900: it is divisible by 4 and gets True, but False was expected.
The function returns True for 1900, but the test expects False.

questions.prompt: Which name best states the behaviour of a test for an order form?
hints: A good name says the situation and the expected result.
questions.onCorrect: A name that states the behaviour makes a failure report readable on its own.

misconceptions.feedback: A number says nothing about the situation or what is expected.
It says only that something is checked, not what or what the result should be.
A noun names a field and not a situation with an expected result.

questions.prompt: A test function contains three assert lines. The first is true, the second is false and the third would be true. How many of the three assert lines run?
hints: What happens to a function when an exception is raised and not caught?
Count the lines up to and including the first failing one.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A failed assertion ends the test, so later asserts in the same test are never reached; one behaviour per test avoids hiding results this way.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first assert runs and passes, the second runs and raises AssertionError, which ends the test, so the third never runs: 2 lines run.

misconceptions.feedback: The exception raised by the second assert ends the function before the third line.
The second assert runs, and it is the one that fails.
The first assert is the first line of the check and does run.

questions.prompt: Why run the new test against the broken function first?
hints: What would a test that always passes show you?
questions.onCorrect: A test seen to fail for the right reason has shown it can detect that fault.

choices.label: To see the test fail, which shows it can detect this fault.
To make the broken code easier to fix.
Because tests only run on code that fails.

acceptedIdeas: To see the test fail, which shows it can detect this fault.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To see the test fail, which shows it can detect this fault.

misconceptions.feedback: The broken function is not changed by running the test; the point is what the test does with it.
Tests run on any code; the question is whether this one can tell good from bad.
Coverage is not involved; the aim is to show that the test can fail.

questions.prompt: The function age_in_years(born) returns date.today().year - born, and a test asserts that age_in_years(1990) == 36. On 1 January 2027, what does age_in_years(1990) return?
hints: Which year does date.today().year give on 1 January 2027?
Subtract 1990.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The test passed in 2026 and fails in 2027 with no change to the code, because it depends on the clock.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: date.today().year is 2027 on that day, and 2027 − 1990 = 37, which is not 36, so the assertion fails.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 2026 result, when the test was written. The clock now gives 2027.
2027 is the current year; the function subtracts the birth year from it.

hints: range(1896, 1905) stops before 1905.
Check 1900 against the century rule.
True counts as 1 in a sum.
questions.onCorrect: Python adds True as 1, so the sum counts the leap years in the range.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: range(1896, 1905) covers 1896 to 1904. Leap years among them are 1896 and 1904, while 1900 is a century not divisible by 400, so the sum counts 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts 1900, which the century rule excludes.
1904 is also divisible by 4 and is not a century.

questions.prompt: What word describes a test that, for the same code, always gives the same result whatever the time, order or network?
hints: The word names a process with no chance in it.
questions.onCorrect: A deterministic test depends only on its code and its inputs, so a failure always means something changed.

misconceptions.feedback: A flaky test is the opposite: it sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code.

questions.prompt: A suite has 8 tests. Three of them contain assertions that are always true, such as assert x == x. How many of the 8 tests are able to detect a fault?
hints: A test that cannot fail checks nothing.
Subtract the tests that cannot fail.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A test that has never been seen to fail may be one that cannot, which is why the red step matters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three tests with always-true assertions cannot fail, so only the other 8 − 3 = 5 can detect a fault.

misconceptions.feedback: The three always-true assertions cannot fail, so they cannot detect anything.
That is the number that cannot detect faults.

questions.prompt: A function charges the standard rate when age > 18 and age < 65, by mistake. The rule says 18 to 65 inclusive. It is tested at ages 10, 40 and 80, each expecting the right rate for the rule. How many of the three tests fail?
hints: Work out the rate the mistaken code gives for 10, for 40 and for 80.
Compare each with what the rule says.
Which ages does the mistake change?
questions.onCorrect: The mistake moves the edges by one, and tests in the middle of a class cannot see it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 gets the child rate, 40 gets standard, and 80 gets the senior rate, exactly as the rule says, so all three pass and 0 fail. The mistake changes only 18 and 65.

misconceptions.feedback: The mistake changes only ages 18 and 65, and none of these three tests uses them.
All three ages are well inside their classes, where the mistaken code agrees with the rule.

questions.prompt: A form field accepts whole numbers from 1 to 99. Counting numbers below 1, numbers from 1 to 99 and numbers above 99 as the three classes, what is the fewest tests that put one value in every class?
hints: Each class needs at least one test.
One value represents the whole class.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: One value stands for its whole class because the program is meant to treat all of them alike.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three classes need one value each, so 3 tests suffice.

misconceptions.feedback: There are 99 valid values, but they all belong to one class and are meant to behave the same.
There are three classes, and each needs a representative.

questions.prompt: What is a value called that sits exactly where the program's behaviour changes, such as 18 in the age rule?
hints: The same word names the line between two classes.
questions.onCorrect: Boundary values are the inputs where off-by-one mistakes in a comparison show up.

misconceptions.feedback: An outlier is an unusual observation in data. A boundary is where behaviour changes.

questions.prompt: Ages 18 to 65 inclusive pay the standard rate. The three-value method tests below, at and above each edge, without repeating a value. How many tests is that?
hints: List the three values around 18, then around 65.
Check whether any value appears in both lists.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The two edges are far apart, so their neighbours do not overlap and the three-value method gives 3 + 3 = 6 values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Edge 18 gives 17, 18 and 19. Edge 65 gives 64, 65 and 66. The six values are distinct, so 6 tests.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the two-value method, which omits 19 and 64.
9 would treat the middle and extremes as extra; the three-value method uses only the values next to each edge.

questions.prompt: The age rule has three valid classes. Add three invalid classes: a negative number, text that is not a number, and empty input. How many classes are there in all?
hints: Add the valid and the invalid classes.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Invalid input needs an expected result too, such as an error message, and is often where the defects are.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 valid classes + 3 invalid classes = 6, and each needs at least one test.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the valid classes. The question includes the three invalid ones.

questions.prompt: A decision table has three yes/no conditions. How many columns does it need to list every combination?
hints: Each condition doubles the number of combinations.
Multiply the number of values of each condition.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The columns grow as a power of two, which is why decision tables are kept to a few conditions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each condition has two values and they combine independently: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the values, 2 + 2 + 2. The combinations multiply.
Two values per condition give 2 x 2 x 2, not 3 x 3.

questions.prompt: A bulk discount applies to orders of 100 items or more. Using the two-value method (just below and at the edge), how many boundary tests are there?
hints: How many edges does the rule have?
Take the value just below and the value at each edge.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A one-sided rule has one boundary; a range has two, which gives four boundary tests.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There is only one edge, at 100, so the two-value method gives 99 and 100: 2 tests.

misconceptions.feedback: Four is for a range with two edges. This rule has only one.
The value at the edge and the value just below it are both needed.

questions.prompt: A month number must be from 1 to 12 inclusive. Using the three-value method, how many boundary tests are there (below, at and above each edge, without repeats)?
hints: List the three values around each edge.
Check for repeated values.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: With a wide range the neighbours of the two edges do not overlap, so the count is 3 per edge.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The edge 1 gives 0, 1 and 2, and the edge 12 gives 11, 12 and 13. The six values are distinct: 6 tests.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the two-value method. The three-value method also tests 2 and 11.
That counts one edge only.

questions.prompt: A test set for ages 18 to 65 is 10, 17, 18, 40, 65, 66 and 90. How many of these seven could be dropped while still covering every class and testing each of the four edge values 17, 18, 65 and 66?
hints: Which four values must stay?
Do those four cover all three classes?
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The edge values do double duty, since each is also a member of its class.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four edge values 17, 18, 65 and 66 already put a value in every class, so 10, 40 and 90 can be dropped: 3.

misconceptions.feedback: Check whether 40 and 10 are needed once 17, 18, 65 and 66 are kept.
Four values must stay, namely 17, 18, 65 and 66. Count how many of the seven are left.

questions.prompt: A decision table has four yes/no conditions. How many columns does it need to list every combination?
hints: Each condition doubles the table.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Sixteen columns for four conditions is why larger rules are split into smaller tables.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for three conditions. A fourth doubles it.
That is 2 x 2 for two conditions.

questions.prompt: In the loan table the income cut-off is 20,000 pounds, counted in whole pounds, and incomes of 20,000 or more count as high. Which income is the value just below the edge?
hints: Subtract the smallest step in the data from the cut-off.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Together with 20,000 itself, 19,999 forms the pair that detects a wrong comparison in the income test.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The value just below 20,000 in whole pounds is 19,999.

misconceptions.feedback: That is far below the edge. The value just below is one step away.
That is above the edge.

questions.prompt: In the function f shown above, the six lines are r = 0, if a, r += 1, if b, r += 2 and return r. A single call f(True, False) is made. How many of the six lines run?
hints: Follow the call: which if conditions are true?
A line inside an if runs only when its condition is true.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Five of six lines gives 83% line coverage, while only two of the four branch outcomes were taken.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lines r = 0, if a, r += 1, if b and return r run. The line r += 2 is skipped because b is False, so 5 lines run.

misconceptions.feedback: The line r += 2 sits under if b, and b is False in this call.
Count the two if lines themselves as lines that run.

questions.prompt: Two calls are made: f(True, True) and f(False, False). What percentage of the four branch outcomes do they take?
hints: List the outcome of each if for each call.
The four outcomes are a true, a false, b true and b false.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Two well-chosen calls can reach every branch outcome, though neither call alone does.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first call takes a true and b true. The second takes a false and b false. Together all 4 outcomes are taken: 100%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure for f(True, True) alone. The second call takes the other two outcomes.
Each call takes two different outcomes, so the pair of them covers all four.

questions.prompt: A suite reaches 100% line coverage, but none of its tests contains an assertion. What does that tell you?
hints: What can a test without an assertion detect?
questions.onCorrect: Coverage measures which code ran, so a suite without assertions can reach any figure and still detect nothing.

choices.label: The code ran, not that it behaved correctly

acceptedIdeas: The code ran, not that it behaved correctly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The code ran, not that it behaved correctly

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing checks the results, so a wrong result cannot make a test fail.
Line coverage can be complete while some branch outcomes are never taken, as with f(True, True).
Without assertions no test can fail, so every mutant survives.

questions.prompt: What is the name for a copy of the code in which one small deliberate change has been made, such as turning > into >=?
hints: The word is the same as in biology: a changed copy.
questions.onCorrect: If a test fails on a mutant it has killed it, and if every test passes the mutant has survived.

misconceptions.feedback: A bug is an unintended defect. A mutant is a change made deliberately to see whether tests notice.
A stub is a stand-in for a dependency, which is a different idea.

questions.prompt: In the table, six of the eight mutants are killed by the one test. What is the mutation score as a percentage?
hints: Mutation score = killed ÷ total mutants, written as a percentage.
Count the rows marked killed.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The two survivors replaced a condition with True, which f(True, True) cannot distinguish from the original.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The score is killed divided by total: 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75, which is 75%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number killed. The score is a percentage of all 8.
That is the share that survived. The score counts those killed.

questions.prompt:
def sign(x):
    if x > 0: return 1
    elif x < 0: return -1
    else: return 0
The tests call sign(5) and sign(-2). The two decisions, x > 0 and x < 0, have four outcomes in all. What percentage of them are taken?
hints: List which outcomes sign(5) takes, then which sign(-2) takes.
x < 0 is only tested when x > 0 is false.
Count the distinct outcomes taken and divide by 4.
questions.onCorrect: The untaken outcome, x < 0 false, is the call sign(0), and without it the else branch never runs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: sign(5) takes x > 0 true. sign(-2) takes x > 0 false and x < 0 true. The outcome x < 0 false is never taken, so 3 of 4 = 75%.

misconceptions.feedback: The else branch, which returns 0, is never reached by 5 or -2.
The pair takes three of the four outcomes, since sign(-2) takes two of them.

questions.prompt:
def f(a, b):
    r = 0
    if a: r += 1
    if b: r += 2
    return r
A single test calls f(True, True). What percentage of branch outcomes is covered?
hints: There are two ifs, each with a true and a false outcome.
How many different outcomes does the single call take?
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Every line ran, yet half of the branch outcomes were never taken, so branch coverage is the stricter measure.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The call takes a true and b true, which is 2 of the 4 outcomes: 50%.

misconceptions.feedback: The lines all run, but the false outcomes of both ifs are never taken.
The call takes one outcome from each if, which is two outcomes in total.

questions.prompt: A tool generates 40 mutants and the tests kill 34 of them. What is the mutation score as a percentage?
hints: Divide the killed mutants by all mutants.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The six survivors point at conditions or values that no assertion checks, and each is a prompt for a new test.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of survivors. The score is a percentage of the killed.
That is the share that survived.

questions.prompt: A suite has a mutation score of 70% over 20 mutants. How many mutants survived?
hints: First find how many were killed: 70% of 20.
Subtract that from 20.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Each survivor is either a missing test or an equivalent mutant whose behaviour is the same as the original's.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 70% of 20 is 14 killed, so 20 − 14 = 6 survived.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number killed.
The score counts a share of 20 mutants, so no more than 20 survivors are possible.

questions.prompt: A test of greeting() asserts the result is 'Good morning', and greeting() reads the real clock and answers 'Good morning' before 12:00. The test runs at every whole hour from 08:00 to 17:00 inclusive. How many of those runs pass?
hints: List the hours at which the test runs.
Which of them are before 12:00?
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The test is correct in the morning and wrong in the afternoon with no change in the code, because the clock is a hidden input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The runs at 08, 09, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17 number 10. Only the first four are before 12:00, so 4 pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of runs. Only those before 12:00 pass.
The run at 12:00 is not before 12, so greeting() says 'Good afternoon' then.
Count only the hours before 12:00, which are 8, 9, 10 and 11.

questions.prompt: What is the name for passing a unit's dependencies in as arguments, instead of letting it create or find them itself?
hints: The dependencies are injected from outside.
questions.onCorrect: Injection can be as simple as an extra parameter, as with the now argument.

misconceptions.feedback: Inheritance shares behaviour between classes. This is about handing a unit what it needs.
Mocking is one use of the result. The practice of passing dependencies in is named differently.

questions.prompt: A dependency always returns the same canned value so that the unit can be tested. This is a:
hints: Which double only supplies answers?
questions.onCorrect: A stub supplies answers and does not check how it was called.

misconceptions.feedback: A mock also checks which calls were made, and nothing here checks the calls.
A spy records the calls it receives, which is not the same as returning canned data.
A fixture is the fixed state that a test starts from, which is different from a stand-in for a dependency.

questions.prompt: A fake repository stores users in a dictionary keyed by id. The test calls add(1, 'a'), add(2, 'b') and then add(1, 'c'), which replaces the entry for id 1. What is len(repo.users) at the end?
hints: A dictionary holds one value for each key.
What does storing under an existing key do?
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A dictionary-backed fake behaves like a table with a primary key: adding with an existing id replaces the row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first two calls create entries 1 and 2. The third replaces the entry for key 1 and adds none, so 2 entries remain.

misconceptions.feedback: Storing under key 1 a second time replaces the old value instead of adding a new entry.
Two of the calls use different keys, and each of those keeps its own entry.

questions.prompt: A spy mailer keeps every message in a list called sent. signup('Ada') and signup('Grace') each send one welcome message. What is len(mailer.sent) afterwards?
hints: Each signup sends one message.
The spy records every message it receives.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The test can now assert on the recorded messages, and the real mail server is never contacted.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each signup sends one message and the spy records each of them, so the list holds 2 messages.

misconceptions.feedback: The spy records every call, so both signups appear in the list.
The spy does not suppress the calls; it records them.

questions.prompt: A test that calls a real network service takes 400 ms, and the same test with a stub takes 2 ms. How many seconds does a suite of 500 such tests save?
hints: Find the saving for one test.
Multiply by 500, then convert milliseconds to seconds.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Speed is not the only gain: a stub also removes failures caused by the network being down.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each test saves 400 − 2 = 398 ms, and 500 × 398 ms = 199,000 ms, which is 199 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure in milliseconds. Divide by 1,000 to get seconds.
The saving per test is 398 ms, not 400, because the stubbed test still takes 2 ms.

questions.prompt: An in-memory dictionary that behaves like a database table is a:
hints: It has working behaviour, only simpler than the real thing.
questions.onCorrect: A fake is a lightweight working implementation, such as an in-memory repository.

misconceptions.feedback: A stub only returns canned answers. This one stores and retrieves what it is given.
A mock verifies calls made to it, which is not what a working in-memory store does.
A driver calls the code under test from above; it is not a stand-in for a dependency.

hints: How many times is price called?
The stub gives the same value each time.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The stub fixes the dependency's answers, so the test checks only the arithmetic of total.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The stub returns 4 for each of the three items, and 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price of one item. total adds the prices of all three.
That is the number of items, not their total price.

questions.prompt: What is a test double called that also checks how it was called, for example that it was called exactly once with a given argument?
hints: It is a double that fails the test if the calls are wrong.
questions.onCorrect: A mock verifies interactions; use it sparingly, because it ties the test to how the code works.

misconceptions.feedback: A stub only returns canned answers and checks nothing about the calls.
A spy records calls for the test to inspect afterwards, and does not fail by itself.

questions.prompt: The faulty function my_sort(xs) returns sorted(set(xs)), which removes duplicates. What does len(my_sort([2, 1, 2])) return?
hints: set() removes repeated values.
Count the items left after set() is applied.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The single example test with [3, 1, 2] never showed this, because that list has no repeated value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: set([2, 1, 2]) holds {1, 2}, and sorted of that is [1, 2], whose length is 2. The input had 3 items, so the length is wrong.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the length of the input. set() removes the repeated value before sorting.
Only the duplicate is removed; both distinct values remain, so count them.

questions.prompt:
Run this code and give the value printed.
x = [3, 1, 2]
print(sorted(sorted(x)) == sorted(x))
hints: Sort x once, then sort the result.
Does sorting an already sorted list change it?
questions.onCorrect: Sorting is idempotent: applying it to its own output changes nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: sorted(x) is [1, 2, 3], and sorting that again gives [1, 2, 3], so the two sides are equal.

questions.prompt: The property len(my_sort(x)) == len(x) fails for [5, 2, 8, 2, 9] because the function drops duplicates. How many items does the smallest failing list have?
hints: What must a list contain for duplicates to be dropped?
Can a list with fewer items fail?
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A shrunk failure shows only what matters: here, two equal values and nothing else.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A duplicate needs at least two equal items, and a list of two equal items such as [0, 0] already fails: 2 items.

misconceptions.feedback: A list with one item has no duplicate to drop, so it passes.
A three-item list with a repeat still fails, but a shorter list fails as well.

questions.prompt: What does shrinking do?
hints: What would you want to hand to a developer after a failure?
questions.onCorrect: A minimal failing input is easier to read and diagnose than the first random one that failed.

choices.label: Reduces a failing input to a minimal one

acceptedIdeas: Reduces a failing input to a minimal one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reduces a failing input to a minimal one

misconceptions.feedback: Shrinking does not touch the tests. It works on the input that made one fail.
Shrinking has nothing to do with log size; it reduces the failing input.
Shrinking runs after a failure and takes extra time; its aim is a smaller input.

questions.prompt:
def bad_reverse(x): return x[:0:-1]  # drops the first item
For x = [3, 1, 2], bad_reverse(x) is [2, 1]. What is len(bad_reverse(bad_reverse(x)))?
hints: Apply bad_reverse to the list that the first call returned.
x[:0:-1] drops the first item and reverses the rest.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Reversing twice should return the original three items, so the length of 1 shows that the round-trip property fails.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first call gives [2, 1]. Applied again it drops the first item of that list, leaving [1], whose length is 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original length, which a correct reverse would restore. bad_reverse loses an item each time.
After the first call the list has 2 items, and the second call drops one more.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the short written mission that gives an exploratory testing session its focus?
hints: It states what to explore and why.
questions.onCorrect: A charter and a time box give exploratory testing structure without scripting the steps.

misconceptions.feedback: A script fixes the steps in advance, which is what exploratory testing leaves open.
A test plan is wider than one session. The one-session mission has its own name.

questions.prompt:
Run this code and give the value printed.
s = 'a_b c'
enc = s.replace(' ', '_')
dec = enc.replace('_', ' ')
print(dec == s)
hints: Work out enc, then dec, and compare it with s.
The underscore in s already stood for itself.
questions.onCorrect: The round trip fails for inputs that already contain an underscore, which is the sort of case a generator finds and an example test seldom tries.

misconceptions.feedback: enc is 'a_b_c', and dec is 'a b c', which is not 'a_b c'.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a property of a sort function, rather than a single example?
hints: A property is about every valid input.
questions.onCorrect: A property states something about all inputs, so a generator can check it on as many as time allows.

choices.label: Sorting any list twice gives the same result as sorting it once
Sorting a list of 1,000 numbers takes under a second

acceptedIdeas: Sorting any list twice gives the same result as sorting it once
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sorting any list twice gives the same result as sorting it once

misconceptions.feedback: That is one example of an input and its output, and it says nothing about other lists.
That is also a single example, an empty list.
That is a performance expectation and not a statement about the result for every input.

questions.prompt: A property test generates 100 inputs each run, and a suite has 8 property tests. How many generated inputs does one run of the suite check?
hints: Each test generates 100 inputs.
Multiply by the number of tests.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Eight tests of this kind check far more inputs than eight example tests would, with the same effort to write.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 inputs × 8 tests = 800 generated inputs.

misconceptions.feedback: The inputs are generated for each test separately, so the counts multiply.
There are 8 tests, each with its own 100 inputs.

questions.prompt:
Run this code and give the value printed.
x = [3, 1, 2]
print(x[::-1][::-1] == x)
hints: Reverse once, then reverse the result.
questions.onCorrect: Reversing twice returns the original, which is a round-trip property.

misconceptions.feedback: Reversing the reversed list returns the original order, so the two sides are equal.

questions.prompt:
def fizz(n): return 'Fizz' if n % 3 == 0 else str(n)
How many of fizz(1) through fizz(15) are equal to 'Fizz'?
hints: List the multiples of 3 up to 15.
15 is also a multiple of 3.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Fizz appears every third number, and 15 is among them, which the later cycle about FizzBuzz has to handle.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The multiples of 3 from 1 to 15 are 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15, so 5 results are 'Fizz'.

misconceptions.feedback: 15 is divisible by 3, so it counts too.
That counts the multiples of five instead. Count those of three.

questions.prompt: What is the first step of test-driven development?
hints: The cycle is red, green, refactor.
questions.onCorrect: Starting with a failing test makes sure that the test is seen to fail before any code satisfies it.

misconceptions.feedback: The code comes after a test that asks for it.
Refactoring comes last in each cycle, once the tests are green.
Nothing is deployed until the cycle is complete and the tests pass.

questions.prompt: This is the code after cycle 2: def fizzbuzz(n): if n % 3 == 0: return 'Fizz'; return str(n). Three tests assert fizzbuzz(3) == 'Fizz', fizzbuzz(1) == '1' and fizzbuzz(5) == 'Buzz'. How many of the three pass?
hints: Evaluate each call against the two lines of code.
5 is not a multiple of 3.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The failing third test is the red step of the next cycle, and it states the next behaviour to add.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: fizzbuzz(3) gives 'Fizz' and fizzbuzz(1) gives '1', so those pass. fizzbuzz(5) gives '5', not 'Buzz', so 2 pass and the next cycle starts red.

misconceptions.feedback: fizzbuzz(5) returns '5' with this code, since 5 is not a multiple of 3 and there is no rule for 5 yet.
Both the first and the second test pass; only the one for 5 fails.

questions.prompt: After the refactoring, fizzbuzz must still give the same results. For n from 1 to 15, how many results are not just the number as text?
hints: Count the multiples of 3 and of 5 between 1 and 15.
15 belongs to both lists, so do not count it twice.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A refactoring test set such as this one checks that every result stayed the same, which is what makes the change safe.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Multiples of 3 number 5 and multiples of 5 number 3, and 15 is in both lists, so 5 + 3 − 1 = 7 results are Fizz, Buzz or FizzBuzz.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts 15 twice, once as a multiple of 3 and once as a multiple of 5.
That adds the multiples of 3 and 5 as 6 + 3; there are 5 multiples of 3 up to 15, including 15.

questions.prompt: The buggy function is def total(price, pct): after = price * (100 - pct) // 100; return after * (100 - pct) // 100, which applies the discount twice. What does total(200, 50) return?
hints: Apply the discount once to find after.
Apply the same discount to after.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The test asserting 100 fails with 50, which is the red step for this bug.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first discount gives 200 × 50 // 100 = 100, and the second gives 100 × 50 // 100 = 50. The expected value is 100.

misconceptions.feedback: 100 is the correct value, which a single discount gives. The buggy code applies the discount again to that value.
The discount is subtracted as a percentage, not as a number of pounds; apply it twice.

questions.prompt: Using the same buggy total(price, pct), which applies the discount twice, what does total(300, 20) return?
hints: Compute the price after one discount.
Apply 80 percent of that again, with whole-number division.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A regression test with these numbers would also fail on the old code, so it can detect the return of the bug.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first discount gives 300 × 80 // 100 = 240, and the second gives 240 × 80 // 100 = 192, where the correct answer is 240.

misconceptions.feedback: 240 is the correct total after one discount. The faulty code discounts again.
That subtracts 20 percent of 300 twice from the original price. The second discount applies to the reduced price.

questions.prompt:
def fizz(n): return 'Fizz' if n % 3 == 0 else str(n)
How many of the results of fizz(i) for i from 1 to 6 are equal to 'Fizz'?
hints: Which of 1 to 6 are divisible by 3?
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The results for 1 to 6 are '1', '2', 'Fizz', '4', '5', 'Fizz'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only 3 and 6 are multiples of 3, so 2 of the six results are 'Fizz'.

misconceptions.feedback: Count the multiples of 3 up to 6 only.
Both 3 and 6 are multiples of 3.

questions.prompt: A bug is reported and fixed. What stops it returning?
hints: What can turn red when behaviour changes?
questions.onCorrect: A regression test written to fail on the bug turns red if a later change brings it back.

choices.label: A regression test that fails before the fix
A manual check before each release

acceptedIdeas: A regression test that fails before the fix
