answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A regression test that fails before the fix

misconceptions.feedback: A comment describes the problem and cannot fail when the bug comes back.
A manual check depends on someone remembering to do it each time.
Ownership assigns responsibility but does not detect a change in behaviour.

questions.prompt: What is the name for changing the structure of code without changing what it does, done while the tests stay green?
hints: It is the third step of red, green, refactor.
questions.onCorrect: Refactoring changes structure only, and the tests are the evidence that behaviour did not change.

misconceptions.feedback: Debugging finds and removes a fault, which does change behaviour.
Optimisation aims at speed or size and is also kept separate from adding behaviour.

questions.prompt: Suite A has 1,000 unit tests of 5 ms each. Suite B has 50 end-to-end tests of 20 s each. How many times longer does suite B take to run than suite A?
hints: Work out each suite's total time in the same unit.
Divide the longer time by the shorter.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A suite with fewer tests can run much longer, because the cost per test differs by a factor of four thousand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Suite A takes 1,000 × 5 ms = 5 s. Suite B takes 50 × 20 s = 1,000 s. The ratio is 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the number of tests, 1,000, by the number of tests, 50; the question compares the total times.
That is the length of suite B in seconds, not the ratio.

questions.prompt: What is the name for a test that drives a whole user journey through the real system, from the interface to the data store?
hints: It runs from one end of the system to the other.
questions.onCorrect: End-to-end tests are the most realistic and the slowest, so a suite keeps few of them.

misconceptions.feedback: A unit test exercises one piece alone, with its dependencies replaced.
An integration test combines a few pieces, but not usually the whole user journey.

questions.prompt: 50 end-to-end tests each take 20 seconds. How many minutes do they take in total? Give the answer to one decimal place.
hints: First find the total in seconds.
Divide the seconds by 60.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: At nearly seventeen minutes the run is too slow to repeat on every change, which is why the pyramid keeps such tests few.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total in seconds. Convert to minutes by dividing by 60.
The total is 1,000 seconds, and 1,000 ÷ 60 is more than ten.

questions.prompt: Each of 50 independent tests has a 1% chance of failing falsely in a run. What is the chance that a run has at least one false failure, as a percentage to one decimal place?
hints: Find the chance that all 50 tests pass, which is 0.99 multiplied by itself 50 times.
Subtract that from 1.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A rate that looks negligible per test becomes a failure in two runs out of five, because the chances compound across the suite.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All 50 pass with probability 0.99^50 = 0.605, so at least one fails with probability 1 − 0.605 = 0.395, which is 39.5%.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 1% fifty times. The chances do not simply add, since two false failures in one run are counted once.
That is the chance that all 50 tests pass; the question asks for at least one failure.

questions.prompt: The same 1% flake rate applies to a suite of 100 independent tests. What is the chance that a run has at least one false failure, as a percentage to one decimal place?
hints: Find 0.99 raised to the power 100.
Subtract that from 1 to get the chance of at least one failure.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Doubling the suite takes the chance of a false red from about two in five to nearly two in three.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All 100 pass with probability 0.99^100 = 0.366, so at least one fails with probability 1 − 0.366 = 0.634, which is 63.4%.

misconceptions.feedback: A suite of 100 tests does not make a false failure certain at 1% each.
That is the chance that every test passes.

questions.prompt: What is a test called that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code?
hints: It is unreliable without any change to the code.
questions.onCorrect: A flaky test erodes trust, because a failure no longer reliably signals a defect.

misconceptions.feedback: A consistently failing test is not flaky, since it gives the same result every run.
A regression test is one written for a fixed bug, which can itself be flaky or stable.

questions.prompt: 20 of the 50 end-to-end tests, at 20 s each, are replaced by 20 unit tests of 5 ms each. How many seconds does the suite save? Give the answer to one decimal place.
hints: Find the time of the 20 slow tests, then the time of the 20 fast ones.
Subtract the second from the first.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Moving a check down the pyramid saves most of its time and also makes a failure easier to locate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 20 end-to-end tests took 20 × 20 s = 400 s. The unit tests take 20 × 0.005 s = 0.1 s. The saving is 400 − 0.1 = 399.9 s.

misconceptions.feedback: The unit tests are not free; 20 of them take 0.1 s, so the saving is a little less than 400.
That is the time the unit tests take, not the time saved.

questions.prompt: 40 end-to-end tests each take 30 seconds. How many minutes do they take in total?
hints: Multiply the number of tests by the time of each.
Convert seconds to minutes.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Twenty minutes for forty tests shows why a team limits end-to-end tests to the critical journeys.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total in seconds. Divide by 60 for minutes.
That adds the 40 and the 30; the total multiplies them.

questions.prompt: Each of 20 independent tests has a 2% chance of a false failure in a run. What is the chance of at least one false failure in a run, as a percentage to one decimal place?
hints: Find the chance that all 20 pass: 0.98 multiplied 20 times.
Subtract from 1.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Even twenty tests with a 2% rate give a false failure about one run in three.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All 20 pass with probability 0.98^20 = 0.668, so at least one fails with probability 1 − 0.668 = 0.332, which is 33.2%.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 2% by 20, which is not how independent chances combine; failures are counted once per run.
That is the chance that every test passes.

questions.prompt: Which test level should have the most tests in a healthy suite?
hints: Which level is fastest and cheapest per test?
questions.onCorrect: Many fast unit tests give quick feedback and point at the failing piece.

misconceptions.feedback: Integration tests need more set-up each, so fewer of them are affordable than of the cheapest kind.
End-to-end tests are the slowest and most brittle, so a healthy suite keeps these fewest.
Manual sessions are useful but limited by people's time, so they cannot be the bulk of the suite.

questions.prompt: A table of customers has four rows with the emails a@x, b@x, a@x and c@x. Each email is meant to appear once. How many rows must be removed to meet that rule?
hints: Which email appears more than once?
How many surplus rows does it have?
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The count of surplus rows is the number of rows minus the number of distinct emails.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The email a@x appears twice, so one of those rows is surplus. The other emails each appear once, so 1 row must be removed.

misconceptions.feedback: Both rows with a@x cannot go; one of them should stay.
That is the number of distinct emails, not the number of surplus rows.

questions.prompt: Table c(email) holds x@y, x@y, z@y, z@y, z@y, w@y. What does SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT email) FROM c; return?
hints: Count all the rows, then count the distinct emails.
Subtract the second from the first.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The difference is the number of surplus rows: one extra x@y and two extra z@y.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: COUNT(*) is 6 and there are 3 distinct emails, so the result is 6 − 3 = 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is COUNT(*), the number of rows. The distinct count is subtracted from it.
That is the number of emails that repeat, not the number of surplus rows.

questions.prompt: An orders table holds 5 orders. A client sends POST /orders, which creates a new order, and its network library retries the request until three requests have succeeded. How many orders does the table hold afterwards?
hints: Does each POST create something new?
Add the successful requests to the existing orders.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A retried POST can duplicate data, which is why such requests are often given an idempotency key.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each successful POST creates a new order, so 5 + 3 = 8 orders. POST is not idempotent, whereas repeating a PUT of the same data leaves the same state.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only one of the three requests, whereas each success adds an order.
That is the count before the requests; each successful POST creates a new order.

questions.prompt: A provider renames a response field. Which test catches this before release?
hints: Which test compares what each side expects of the messages?
questions.onCorrect: A contract test fails in the provider's build when its response no longer matches what a consumer expects.

choices.label: A unit test of the consumer's logic only

misconceptions.feedback: A unit test of the consumer's logic uses a double for the provider, so the rename never reaches it.
A load test measures behaviour under demand and does not compare field names.
A usability test examines how people use the product, which is not where a field rename is found.

questions.prompt: A client retries the same PUT request three times, and the data ends in the same state as after one request. What word describes this property?
hints: It is the property that repeating an operation has no further effect.
questions.onCorrect: Idempotent requests are safe to retry, which matters when networks drop replies.

misconceptions.feedback: Atomic means all or nothing; it says nothing about repeating a request.
Stateless means the server keeps nothing between requests, a different idea.

questions.prompt: Table c(email) holds a@x, b@x, a@x, c@x. Run: SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT email) FROM c; What is returned?
hints: Count all the rows and the distinct emails.
Subtract.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A result above zero means the uniqueness rule is broken.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: COUNT(*) is 4 and COUNT(DISTINCT email) is 3, so the difference is 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of distinct emails.
That is the number of rows.

questions.prompt: A table has 5 rows, and the email column is NULL in 2 of them. A not-null check returns the rows where email IS NULL. How many rows does it return?
hints: Which rows break a not-null rule?
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Note that COUNT(email) would return 3, because it skips NULLs, so it hides the violations that the check is looking for.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The check returns exactly the rows that violate the rule, which are the 2 rows with a NULL email.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows that have an email. The check returns the rows that do not.
That is every row in the table.

questions.prompt: Why should each test create its own data?
hints: What happens when one test changes what another reads?
questions.onCorrect: Tests that share mutable data can pass or fail depending on the order they run in.

choices.label: To avoid order-dependent failures from shared state

acceptedIdeas: To avoid order-dependent failures from shared state
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To avoid order-dependent failures from shared state

misconceptions.feedback: Creating data per test is usually slightly slower, so speed is not the reason.
Storage is not the concern; tests share nothing so that they cannot interfere.
Per-test data still needs to be removed or discarded, so cleanup is not avoided.

questions.prompt: Run the check on the four rows a@x, b@x, a@x and c@x. SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; How many rows does it return?
hints: Which groups have more than one row?
Count those groups, not the rows inside them.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The query returns one row per duplicated email, not one row per surplus customer.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the group a@x has more than one row, so the check returns 1 row.

misconceptions.feedback: The group a@x holds two customers, but the query returns one row for the group.
A result of zero would mean the rule holds, and a@x appears twice.

questions.prompt: The twenty response times in ms, sorted, are 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 24, 26, 29, 33, 41, 58, 120 and 450. Work out the mean, and then count how many of the twenty requests are slower than it.
hints: Add the twenty times and divide by 20.
Then count the times larger than the mean.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Seventeen of twenty requests were faster than the mean, so it describes few of them well.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sum is 976 ms and the mean is 976 ÷ 20 = 48.8 ms. Only 58, 120 and 450 exceed it, so 3 requests are slower.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of requests faster than the mean. The question asks for those slower.
Two other requests besides the slowest are slower than the mean.

questions.prompt: By nearest rank, what is the 90th percentile of the same twenty times, in ms? Use the sorted list above.
hints: Rank = the percentile as a fraction, times the number of values, rounded up.
Count along the sorted list to that rank.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Nine in ten of the requests took 58 ms or less, a much better description of the slow end than the mean.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rank is ceil(0.90 × 20) = 18, and the 18th value of the sorted list is 58 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean. A percentile is a value from the list at a given rank.
That is the 19th value, the 95th percentile. The 90th percentile has rank 18.

questions.prompt: A service receives 120 requests per second and each spends 0.5 s in the system on average. How many requests are in flight on average?
hints: Little's law: in flight = arrival rate × average time in the system.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The same law can be turned round: with 60 slots and 0.5 s each, the system can sustain at most 120 requests a second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Little's law gives L = 120 × 0.5 = 60 requests.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the rate by the time. Little's law multiplies them.
That is the arrival rate alone.

questions.prompt: What is the name for a test that raises the load beyond the expected demand in order to find where the system breaks?
hints: Expected demand is covered by a load test; this one goes further.
questions.onCorrect: A stress test shows the breaking point and how the system fails, which a load test at expected demand does not.

misconceptions.feedback: A load test applies the demand the system is expected to see, and stays within it.
A soak test holds a normal load for a long time to find slow decay.

questions.prompt: An automated accessibility tool reports no errors on a page. What does that show?
hints: Does automation find everything?
questions.onCorrect: Automated tools find part of the accessibility problems, and the rest need manual checks with people and assistive technology.

choices.label: The page meets every accessibility requirement
No problems that the tool can detect; manual checks are still needed
The page passed a stress test

acceptedIdeas: No problems that the tool can detect; manual checks are still needed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No problems that the tool can detect; manual checks are still needed

misconceptions.feedback: A tool can detect only some kinds of problem, so a clean report is not a full pass.
A stress test concerns load, which accessibility tools do not measure.
A tool does not replace testing with a screen reader, so this is not shown.

questions.prompt: Ten response times in ms, sorted, are 100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150, 160, 170, 180 and 900. By nearest rank, what is the 90th percentile?
hints: Rank = the fraction times the number of values, rounded up.
Count to that rank in the sorted list.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The one slow request of 900 ms barely moves the 90th percentile, but it lifts the mean from 140 to 216.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rank is ceil(0.90 × 10) = 9, and the 9th value is 180 ms. The 900 sits at rank 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 10th value, which would be the 100th percentile.
That is the mean. A percentile is a value in the list at a given rank.

questions.prompt: The same ten times are 100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150, 160, 170, 180 and 900 ms. By nearest rank, what is the 50th percentile in ms?
hints: Rank = 0.5 × 10, rounded up.
Count to that rank.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: By nearest rank the percentile is always a value that appears in the list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rank is ceil(0.50 × 10) = 5, and the 5th value is 140 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 6th value. The rank for the 50th percentile of ten values is 5.
That is the mean, which the 900 ms request pulls upwards.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of the ten response times 100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150, 160, 170, 180 and 900 ms?
hints: Add all ten values.
Divide by 10.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: The mean is above nine of the ten requests, because the single 900 ms request pulls it up.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The nine small values sum to 1,260 and adding 900 gives 2,160; 2,160 ÷ 10 = 216 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 50th percentile by nearest rank, not the mean.
That is the 90th percentile, not the mean.

questions.prompt: A service gets 250 requests per second, and each request spends 0.04 s in the system on average. How many requests are in flight on average?
hints: Multiply the arrival rate by the average time in the system.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Short requests keep concurrency low even at a high arrival rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: L = 250 × 0.04 = 10 requests.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the rate by the time. Little's law multiplies them.
That is the arrival rate alone.

questions.prompt: Which element is most essential to a useful bug report?
hints: What does a developer need before anything else can be done?
questions.onCorrect: A fault that can be reproduced can be investigated, whereas a fault that cannot is usually closed.

choices.label: The reporter's opinion of the developer

misconceptions.feedback: An opinion about a person gives the developer nothing to act on.
A screenshot can help, but without steps it shows what happened and not how to make it happen.
A suggested fix can help, but it assumes a cause that the report has not shown.

questions.prompt: What is the word for the impact of a defect, as distinct from how soon it should be fixed?
hints: The other word, for the order of fixing, is priority.
questions.onCorrect: Severity measures impact and priority sets the order, and they can point in different directions.

misconceptions.feedback: Priority is the order in which defects should be fixed, which depends on more than impact.

questions.prompt: A team found 45 defects before release, and 5 more were reported after release. What percentage of the defects found overall did the team find before release?
hints: Add the defects found before and after.
Divide the number found before by that total.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: This share is called the defect detection percentage, and it can only be settled once the defects after release have been counted.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 45 + 5 = 50, and 45 ÷ 50 = 0.9, which is 90%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number found before release. The question asks for a share of the total.
That is the share found after release, 5 of 50, and not the share found before.

questions.prompt: Team B found 30 defects before release and 20 more were reported after. What is its defect detection percentage?
hints: Total = before + after.
Divide the before count by the total.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Both teams had a total of 50 defects, and Team B's testing caught fewer of them before users did.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 30 + 20 = 50, and 30 ÷ 50 = 0.6, which is 60%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number found before release; divide it by the total.
That is the share found after release.

questions.prompt: Each area gets a risk score, which is likelihood multiplied by impact, each from 1 to 5. Payments have likelihood 2 and impact 5, login has 3 and 4, search has 4 and 2, and the colour theme has 4 and 1. What is the highest score?
hints: Multiply the two numbers for each area.
Compare the four products.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Login ranks above payments here because its failure is more likely, so it gets testing effort first under these scores.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The scores are payments 10, login 12, search 8 and theme 4, so the highest is 12, for login.

misconceptions.feedback: That is payments, whose likelihood is lower than login's.
That adds the two numbers for login. The score is their product.

questions.prompt: What is the name for releasing a new version to a small share of users first, and watching for problems before it goes to everyone?
hints: The name comes from the bird taken into mines to give early warning.
questions.onCorrect: A canary release limits how many users a defect can reach, and monitoring says whether to continue.

misconceptions.feedback: Blue-green releases switch all traffic between two full environments, which differs from sending a small share first.
A rollback undoes a release after a problem has appeared.

questions.prompt: A team made 80 deployments in a month, and 6 of them needed a fix or a rollback. What is its change failure rate, as a percentage to one decimal place?
hints: Divide the failed deployments by all deployments.
Write it as a percentage.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Change failure rate is one of the DORA delivery measures and is read together with how quickly service is restored.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of failures. Divide it by 80.
That is the share of deployments that did not fail.

questions.prompt: 76 defects were found before release and 4 more after. What is the defect detection percentage?
hints: Add before and after for the total.
Divide before by the total.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: A high figure here reflects both thorough testing and the passage of time, since late defects may still arrive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 76 + 4 = 80, and 76 ÷ 80 = 0.95, which is 95%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number found before release.
That is the share found after release.

questions.prompt: A team's defect detection percentage is 80%, and it found 40 defects before release. How many were found after release?
hints: If 40 is 80% of the total, what is the total?
Subtract the 40 found before.
Write down each intermediate value before combining them, and check the units or the sign of each.
questions.onCorrect: Working back from a percentage is a way to check a figure against the raw counts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 is 80% of the total, so the total is 40 ÷ 0.8 = 50, and 50 − 40 = 10 were found after.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total number of defects. The question asks for those found after release.
That takes 80% of 40, but 40 is already the 80% share.

questions.prompt: A misspelt company name on the landing page is best described as:
hints: Is the harm large, and is the fix urgent?
questions.onCorrect: Severity and priority differ here: the impact is small but the page is public, so the fix comes soon.

misconceptions.feedback: The harm to users is small, so severity is low, even though the fix is urgent.
The urgency is high because it is the first thing visitors see.
The fault is cheap to fix and public, so it should not wait.

flashcards.front: What is the source of the expected result in a test called?
flashcards.back: It is the oracle, and it must be independent of the code under test.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the oracle, and it must be independent of the code under test.

flashcards.front: How many input pairs does a function of two 8-bit integers have?
What is the difference between verification and validation?
flashcards.back: Verification checks the product against its specification, and validation checks that the specification meets the need.

flashcards.front: What do the three parts of a unit test stand for, in order?
flashcards.back: Arrange sets up the input, act calls the code once, and assert states the expected result.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Arrange sets up the input, act calls the code once, and assert states the expected result.

flashcards.front: What word means that a test always gives the same result for the same code?
flashcards.back: A deterministic test does not depend on time, order or network, so a failure always means the code changed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A deterministic test does not depend on time, order or network, so a failure always means the code changed.

flashcards.front: Why run a new test against broken code at least once?
flashcards.back: Seeing it fail for the right reason shows that the test can tell good code from bad.

flashcards.front: Ages 18 to 65 inclusive: how many two-value boundary tests are there?
flashcards.back: The edges 18 and 65 give 17, 18, 65 and 66, which is 4 tests.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The edges 18 and 65 give 17, 18, 65 and 66, which is 4 tests.

flashcards.front: What do we call a group of inputs that the program should treat alike?
flashcards.back: An equivalence class, so one test from it stands for all of its members.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An equivalence class, so one test from it stands for all of its members.

flashcards.front: A decision table has 3 yes/no conditions. How many combinations does it have?
flashcards.back: Each condition doubles the count: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each condition doubles the count: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

flashcards.front: What do you call a copy of the code with one small deliberate fault planted in it?
flashcards.back: A mutant, which the suite either kills by failing or lets survive.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A mutant, which the suite either kills by failing or lets survive.

flashcards.front: A suite kills 30 of 40 mutants. What is the mutation score as a percentage?
Why can a suite with 100% line coverage still be poor?
flashcards.back: Coverage records only that code ran, and a test with no assertion checks nothing.

flashcards.front: What is the practice of passing a unit's dependencies in as arguments called?
flashcards.back: It is dependency injection, and it lets a test supply stand-ins for the clock, the network or a database.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is dependency injection, and it lets a test supply stand-ins for the clock, the network or a database.

flashcards.front: What separates a stub from a mock?
flashcards.back: A stub returns canned answers, whereas a mock also checks which calls were made to it.

flashcards.front: What is a simple working in-memory stand-in for a database called?
flashcards.back: A fake, which behaves like the real store but is faster and private to the test.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A fake, which behaves like the real store but is faster and private to the test.

flashcards.front: What do you call a statement that holds for every valid input?
flashcards.back: A property, so it can be checked on any generated input.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A property, so it can be checked on any generated input.

flashcards.front: What is it called when a tool reduces a failing input to the smallest one that still fails?
flashcards.back: Shrinking, which leaves the developer with a minimal counter-example.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shrinking, which leaves the developer with a minimal counter-example.

flashcards.front: What gives an exploratory testing session its structure?
flashcards.back: A charter that says what to explore and a time box that limits it, plus notes.

flashcards.front: What is the name for changing code structure without changing behaviour?
flashcards.back: Refactoring, whose safety depends on the tests staying green.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Refactoring, whose safety depends on the tests staying green.

flashcards.front: Why watch a new test fail before writing the code?
flashcards.back: A test that has never been seen to fail may be unable to fail, so the red step shows that it checks something.

flashcards.front: What do you call a test written from a bug report so that the bug cannot return?
flashcards.back: A regression test, which fails on the buggy code and passes on the fix.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A regression test, which fails on the buggy code and passes on the fix.

flashcards.front: What do you call a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails on the same code?
flashcards.back: A flaky test, which makes failures harder to trust.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A flaky test, which makes failures harder to trust.

flashcards.front: 1,000 unit tests take 5 ms each. How many seconds is that in total?
flashcards.back: 1,000 × 5 ms = 5,000 ms = 5 seconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,000 × 5 ms = 5,000 ms = 5 seconds.

flashcards.front: Why should a healthy suite have more unit tests than end-to-end tests?
flashcards.back: Unit tests are fast, cheap and point at the failing piece, while end-to-end tests are slow, brittle and unspecific.

flashcards.front: What do we call a request that has the same effect when repeated as when sent once?
flashcards.back: It is idempotent, so a lost reply can safely be retried.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is idempotent, so a lost reply can safely be retried.

flashcards.front: A table has 10 rows and 8 distinct emails. What does COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT email) return?
flashcards.back: 10 − 8 = 2 surplus rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 − 8 = 2 surplus rows.

flashcards.front: Why does a contract test catch a renamed field before release?
flashcards.back: The provider runs the consumer's contract against its real responses in its own build, so the mismatch fails there.

flashcards.front: A service handles 100 requests per second with an average time in the system of 0.3 s. How many requests are in flight on average?
flashcards.back: Little's law: L = 100 × 0.3 = 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Little's law: L = 100 × 0.3 = 30.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a test that raises load beyond expected demand to find the breaking point?
flashcards.back: A stress test, which shows where and how the system fails.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A stress test, which shows where and how the system fails.

flashcards.front: Why can the mean response time mislead?
flashcards.back: A few very slow requests pull the mean up past most of the data, and a percentile shows the slow tail directly.

flashcards.front: What is the word for the impact of a defect, as opposed to the order in which it is fixed?
flashcards.back: Severity measures impact, and priority sets the order of fixing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Severity measures impact, and priority sets the order of fixing.

flashcards.front: 40 defects were found before release and 10 after. What is the defect detection percentage?
Why does a team test both early in the pipeline and in production?
flashcards.back: Early tests find defects cheaply, but only real use shows what no test set anticipated.
